papers.abstract_zh: 三重重配的H3N3 禽流感病毒(AIVs)的出现对家禽和公共卫生构成威胁。本研究对中国鸡群中分离的三种新型H3N3病毒株(SQ2049、HN0120和GT2125)进行了表征,评估了它们的进化、致病性和疫苗效果。系统发育分析显示这些病毒株源自H10N3和H3N8谱系,携带H9N2病毒的内部基因组骨架。尽管被鉴定为低致病性AIVs(IVPI=0),但它们表现出不同的复制适应性。GT2125在胚胎中表现出较低的效率,并携带独特的PB2突变(V598I和K702)。在SPF鸡的致病性试验中发现,SQ2049在无临床症状的情况下实现了高效的水平传播,肛门病毒排毒持续了11天,而口腔排毒仅持续2至3天,在气管和免疫器官中观察到轻微的组织病理学病变。重要的是,灭活的SQ2049 疫苗引发了高交叉反应抗体滴度(HI≥8log2)并在SPF鸡中提供了100%的保护效果。在小鼠感染研究中,病毒在小鼠体内复制后发现了两种HA突变(G174E和N209D)。这些两种突变此前曾与哺乳动物适应性和增强对人类型α-2,6受体的结合能力相关,但本研究未评估它们在H3N3背景下的功能效应。这些发现扩展了我们对H3N3 AIV进化动态的理解,并强调了监测对于重配流感病毒的重要性。所展示的疫苗效果为未来H3N3的预防和控制策略奠定了基础。
papers.summary_zh: 三重重配的H3N3 禽流感病毒(AIVs)的出现对家禽和公共卫生构成威胁。本研究对中国鸡群中分离的三种新型H3N3病毒株(SQ2049、HN0120和GT2125)进行了表征,评估了它们的进化、致病性和疫苗效果。系统发育分析显示这些病毒株源自H10N3和H3N8谱系,携带H9N2病毒的内部基因组骨架。尽管被鉴定为低致病性AIVs(IVPI=0),但它们表现出不同的复制适应性。GT2125在胚胎中表现出较低的效率,并携带独特的PB2突变(V598I和K702)。在SPF鸡的致病性试验中发现,SQ2049在无临床症状的情况下实现了高效的水平传播,肛门病毒排毒持续了11天,而口腔排毒仅持续2至3天,在气管和免疫器官中观察到轻微的组织病理学病变。重要的是,灭活的SQ2049 疫苗引发了高交叉反应抗体滴度(HI≥8log2)并在SPF鸡中提供了100%的保护效果。在小鼠感染研究中,病毒在小鼠体内复制后发现了两种HA突变(G174E和N209D)。这些两种突变此前曾与哺乳动物适应性和增强对人类型α-2,6受体的结合能力相关,但本研究未评估它们在H3N3背景下的功能效应。这些发现扩展了我们对H3N3 AIV进化动态的理解,并强调了监测对于重配流感病毒的重要性。所展示的疫苗效果为未来H3N3的预防和控制策略奠定了基础。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估具有哺乳动物适应性突变的新兴H3N3 禽流感病毒的进化、致病性和疫苗效果,因为它们的出现对家禽和公共卫生构成威胁。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究对中国鸡群中分离的三种新型H3N3病毒株(SQ2049、HN0120和GT2125)进行了表征,评估了它们在SPF鸡中的复制适应性和致病性。
analysis_zh.methods: 使用系统发育分析来确定病毒株的起源,并通过SPF鸡的致病性试验评估其复制和排毒模式。此外,还进行了小鼠感染研究以识别与哺乳动物适应性相关的HA突变。
analysis_zh.main_results: SQ2049在无临床症状的情况下在SPF鸡中实现了高效的水平传播,肛门病毒排毒持续了11天,而口腔排毒仅持续2至3天。灭活的SQ2049 疫苗引发了高交叉反应抗体滴度(HI≥8log2)并在SPF鸡中提供了100%的保护效果。GT2125在胚胎中表现出较低的效率,并携带独特的PB2突变(V598I和K702)。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些发现扩展了我们对H3N3 AIV进化动态的理解,并强调了监测对于重配流感病毒的重要性,因为所识别的HA突变此前曾与哺乳动物适应性和增强对人类型α-2,6受体的结合能力相关。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 所展示的疫苗效果为未来H3N3的预防和控制策略奠定了基础,同时本研究强调了对具有潜在人兽共患病能力的禽流感病毒进行持续监测的必要性。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究仅限于SPF鸡和小鼠模型,这可能无法完全代表自然宿主相互作用。证据强度中等,因为未评估HA突变在H3N3背景下的功能效应。

papers.title: Knowledge of Avian Influenza Among Poultry Workers & Development of SIM on Prevention of Avian Influenza
papers.abstract: Avian influenza is an important zoonotic disease of global concern, with poultry workers at particular risk because of their close and frequent contact with birds and contaminated environments. This study assessed the level of knowledge regarding avian influenza among poultry workers in selected poultry farms of Sangli and Miraj city, with a view to developing a self‐instructional module on its prevention. A descriptive cross‐sectional design was used, and 60 poultry workers were selected by simple random sampling from identified farms in the study area. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire consisting of demographic variables and 16 multiple‐choice items covering transmission, clinical manifestations in humans and birds, diagnosis, vaccination, biosecurity measures, safe cooking practices, and use of personal protective equipment. Knowledge scores were categorized as bad, average, good, or excellent. The findings showed that 70% of poultry workers had average knowledge and 30% had good knowledge; none had bad or excellent knowledge. More than half of the workers reported no prior knowledge of avian influenza, and among those who had heard about it, the main sources were social media, newspapers, television, and health workers. Important gaps were observed in the understanding of human‐to‐human transmission, recommended personal protective equipment, appropriate cooking practices, reporting of sick or dead birds, and farm‐level biosecurity. Chi‐square analysis revealed no statistically significant association between knowledge level and selected demographic variables such as age, education, type of work, work experience, and previous knowledge. In response to the identified deficiencies, a self‐instructional module was developed focusing on essential concepts and practical preventive measures. The study highlights the need for simple, locally appropriate educational interventions to strengthen knowledge and promote safer practices among poultry workers, thereby reducing the risk of avian influenza transmission at the human–poultry interface.

source_records.abstract: Avian influenza is an important zoonotic disease of global concern, with poultry workers at particular risk because of their close and frequent contact with birds and contaminated environments. This study assessed the level of knowledge regarding avian influenza among poultry workers in selected poultry farms of Sangli and Miraj city, with a view to developing a self‐instructional module on its prevention. A descriptive cross‐sectional design was used, and 60 poultry workers were selected by simple random sampling from identified farms in the study area. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire consisting of demographic variables and 16 multiple‐choice items covering transmission, clinical manifestations in humans and birds, diagnosis, vaccination, biosecurity measures, safe cooking practices, and use of personal protective equipment. Knowledge scores were categorized as bad, average, good, or excellent. The findings showed that 70% of poultry workers had average knowledge and 30% had good knowledge; none had bad or excellent knowledge. More than half of the workers reported no prior knowledge of avian influenza, and among those who had heard about it, the main sources were social media, newspapers, television, and health workers. Important gaps were observed in the understanding of human‐to‐human transmission, recommended personal protective equipment, appropriate cooking practices, reporting of sick or dead birds, and farm‐level biosecurity. Chi‐square analysis revealed no statistically significant association between knowledge level and selected demographic variables such as age, education, type of work, work experience, and previous knowledge. In response to the identified deficiencies, a self‐instructional module was developed focusing on essential concepts and practical preventive measures. The study highlights the need for simple, locally appropriate educational interventions to strengthen knowledge and promote safer practices among poultry workers, thereby reducing the risk of avian influenza transmission at the human–poultry interface.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to assess the level of knowledge regarding avian influenza among poultry workers in Sangli and Miraj city to develop a self-instructional module on prevention. A descriptive cross-sectional design was employed, involving 60 poultry workers selected through simple random sampling. Data were gathered using a structured questionnaire with 16 multiple-choice items covering various aspects of avian influenza. The results indicated that 70% of participants had average knowledge, while 30% had good knowledge, with no one achieving bad or excellent scores. Over half of the workers had no prior knowledge of avian influenza, and those who were aware primarily obtained information from social media, newspapers, television, and health workers. The study identified significant gaps in understanding key aspects of avian influenza, such as human-to-human transmission, personal protective equipment, cooking practices, and biosecurity measures. These findings underscore the importance of targeted educational interventions to improve knowledge and reduce transmission risks at the human-poultry interface. The study's limitations include the lack of a statistically significant association between knowledge levels and demographic factors, which may affect the generalizability of the results. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational nature of the study and the absence of control groups.

papers.abstract_zh: 禽流感是一种全球关注的重要人兽共患病,禽类从业人员由于与鸟类及污染环境密切频繁接触,面临特别高的风险。本研究评估了在桑利和米尔杰市选定禽类农场中禽类从业人员对禽流感的认知水平,旨在开发一个关于其预防的自我指导模块。采用描述性横断面研究设计,从研究区域中确定的农场中通过简单随机抽样选取了60名禽类从业人员。数据通过结构化问卷收集,问卷包括人口统计学变量和16个关于禽流感、人类和鸟类的临床表现、禽流感病毒的传播、禽流感病毒的变异、禽流感病毒的检测、生物安全措施、安全烹饪实践以及个人防护装备使用情况的多项选择题。认知得分被分为差、一般、好或优秀四个等级。研究结果显示,70%的从业人员认知水平为一般,30%为好;没有人的认知水平为差或优秀。超过一半的从业人员表示此前对禽流感没有了解,而在那些听说过禽流感的人中,主要信息来源是社交媒体、报纸、电视和卫生工作者。在人类间传播、推荐的个人防护装备、适当的烹饪实践、报告生病或死亡的鸟类以及农场层面的生物安全等方面存在重要认知差距。卡方分析显示,认知水平与所选人口统计学变量(如年龄、教育程度、工作类型、工作经验和先前知识)之间没有统计学上的显著关联。针对发现的认知不足,开发了一个聚焦于关键概念和实际预防措施的自我指导模块。本研究强调需要简单且适合当地情况的教育干预措施,以增强禽类从业人员的知识并促进更安全的实践,从而降低人类与禽类接触界面禽流感传播的风险。

papers.title: Territorial risk of high pathogenicity avian influenza in France is associated with farmed species diversity
papers.abstract: Animal infectious diseases threaten food security, livestock production and public health. While disease prevention strategies typically target risk factors associated with high-competence hosts or environmental conditions, we hypothesise that lower-competence species can reduce disease risk by diluting effective contact rates between farms. Using spatial statistical models calibrated on three successive French high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) epidemics (2020-2023), we show that greater local diversity of livestock farms, including cattle and pig farms, is associated with significantly lower HPAI risk. Moreover, we show that the positive association between duck houses and HPAI risk weakens as the number of less-competent non-duck poultry houses increases, revealing a dilution effect within poultry production systems. These findings suggest that livestock diversity is a previously overlooked determinant of disease spread and open new research avenues on territorial diversification to complement traditional approaches for the long-term control of high-impact animal infectious diseases.

Using spatial statistical models calibrated on three successive French high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) epidemics (2020-2023), we show that greater local diversity of livestock farms, including cattle and pig farms, is associated with significantly lower HPAI risk. Moreover, we show that the positive association between duck houses and HPAI risk weakens as the number of less-competent non-duck poultry houses increases, revealing a dilution effect within poultry production systems. These findings suggest that livestock diversity is a previously overlooked determinant of disease spread and open new research avenues on territorial diversification to complement traditional approaches for the long-term control of high-impact animal infectious diseases.

papers.abstract_zh: 动物传染病威胁粮食安全、畜牧业生产和公共卫生。尽管疾病预防策略通常针对与高竞争力宿主或环境条件相关的风险因素,我们假设低竞争力物种可以通过稀释农场间的有效接触率来降低疾病风险。通过使用校准于法国三次连续高致病性禽流感(HPAI)疫情(2020-2023)的空间统计模型,我们发现包括牛场和猪场在内的本地养殖农场多样性与显著降低的HPAI风险相关。此外,我们还发现鸭舍与HPAI风险之间的正相关关系随着低竞争力非鸭类禽舍数量的增加而减弱,揭示了禽类生产系统内的稀释效应。这些发现表明,养殖多样性是之前被忽视的疾病传播决定因素,并为通过地域多样化研究来补充传统方法,以实现对高影响动物传染病的长期控制开辟了新的研究途径。

Volume 32, Number 11—November 2026 Research Letter Evidence of Exposure to Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza H5 Viruses in East Greenland Polar Bears Suggested citation for this article Abstract We detected influenza A virus antibodies in plasma collected from East Greenland polar bears during subsistence hunts in 2024 (3/14 [21%]) and 2025 (6/14 [43%]). Four bears from 2025 had antibodies for the globally emerging highly pathogenic avian influenza virus H5 clade 2.3.4.4b, consistent with survival after exposure. Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) is an emerging ecologic and public health threat in the Arctic (1). Seasonal bird migrations to Arctic nesting grounds create a hot spot for HPAI outbreaks, amplifying interspecies interactions and the risk for viral reassortment and dissemination across migratory flyways (1). Recent detection of HPAI in wild Arctic mammals, along with their nutritional and cultural relevance for Indigenous peoples, emphasizes a strong need for surveillance in Arctic ecosystems (2–4). Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) are Arctic apex predators that face increased challenges associated with their ecologic position at the interface between marine and terrestrial ecosystems. Climate warming and the subsequent loss of sea ice leads to increased time spent on land and exposure to terrestrial pathogens through the exploitation of new food sources (5). Cases of deceased polar bears infected with HPAI have been reported in Alaska, USA (H5N1 in 2023), and Svalbard, Norway (H5N5 in 2026), emphasizing that these emerging viruses may pose a risk to Arctic species (2,6). As part of an ongoing collaboration with Indigenous hunters, heart blood was collected during subsistence harvests from polar bears that appeared healthy near Scoresby Sound (Ittoqqortoormiit) in East Greenland (Appendix Figure) during the hunting season (January–May). We screened 109 plasma samples (collected during 2016–2025) for antibodies against all influenza A viruses by using a competitive ELISA (cELISA) that targets the influenza A virus (IAV) nucleoprotein (ID Screen Influenza A Antibody Competition Multi-Species; Innovative Diagnostics, https://www.innovative-diagnostics.com), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. We detected no IAV antibodies before 2024. Three bears (all male) harvested during 2024 had signal-to-noise values within the positive range (<45%) of the cELISA (21% [95% CI 8%–48%]; n = 3/14); the number increased to 6 bears (5 male, 1 female) in 2025 (43% [95% CI 21%–67%]; n = 6/14) (Appendix Table). We conducted further screening on positive samples (n = 9) and a subset of negative samples (n = 3) by using a hemagglutination inhibition assay that used horse red blood cells (Rockland Immunochemicals, https://www.rockland.com), as described by Kayali et al. (7), with minor modifications. In brief, we heat-inactivated plasma at 56 °C for 30 minutes, then hem-adsorbed it and treated it with receptor-destroying enzyme. We used avian influenza viruses representative of H5 and H7 subtypes in the assay (Table). Plasma from 4 animals harvested in 2025 that were positive for IAV antibodies on the cELISA were positive (>1:40) for antibodies to H5N1 viruses falling within clade 2.3.4.4b on the hemagglutination inhibition assay, suggesting that the animals had been exposed to an HPAI virus in this clade (Table). We first detected IAV antibodies in East Greenland polar bears in 2024 and antibodies to the highly pathogenic H5 clade 2.3.4.4b in 2025. H5N5 and H5N1 strains were previously confirmed in sea birds (including Uria aalge [H5N1 in 2022], Larus hyperboreus [H5N5 in 2023], Fulmarus glacialis [H5N5 in 2023 and 2024], and Larus marinus [H5N5 in 2024]) from the west coast of Greenland (8,9), consistent with our findings of evidence of IAV exposure in East Greenland polar bears in 2024. Positive bears probably were exposed during the summer–fall bird migration the year before the bears were harvested, given that migratory birds are absent during the polar bear hunting season. Hunters reported no clinical signs, suggesting that bears can recover from HPAI infection. That finding is consistent with the high prevalence reported in our study and survival of the bears for months after the departure of migratory birds. Although cross-reactivity with low pathogenic H5 subtypes is possible, plasma from all 4 seropositive bears inhibited hemagglutination of viruses within clade 2.3.4.4b (not observed when tested against clade 1) (Table). That finding strongly supports infection with a virus from clade 2.3.4.4b, which is exclusively an HPAI lineage. HPAI spillover to mammalian hosts typically occurs through ingestion of infected birds or through contaminated environments (1,3,10). Transmission to wild mammals may involve multiple mechanisms, including direct contact through mucosal or nasal secretions, scavenging dead birds or bird eggs or infected mammals, and mother-to-offspring transmission through lactation (Figure) (10). Further studies are needed to identify which mechanisms are relevant for polar bears, although the most likely route is by eating dead or infected birds and mammals. Greenland links the East Atlantic and the North American Atlantic flyways (Appendix Figure), and increased surveillance in this region may provide effective early warning signs of HPAI dissemination. Our findings indicate that East Greenland polar bears have been exposed to HPAI in recent years, consistent with the timeline of prior reports of HPAI in birds along the linked migratory superhighways (3,8,9). This carnivore may be an ideal sentinel for emerging HPAI in Arctic ecosystems, given that polar bears opportunistically scavenge coastal nests, birds, and marine mammals as they face nutritional stress associated with sea ice loss (2,5). Our study also highlights the strength of collaboration between scientists and local subsistence hunters, emphasizing the need for future research that incorporates diverse perspectives and cultural practices to effectively monitor the health of wildlife in these remote regions. Dr. Buhler is a researcher at the University of Inland Norway and a postdoctoral fellow at the Cornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Wildlife Health at Cornell University. Her research interests include the epidemiology and ecology of zoonotic pathogens, using a One Health approach to investigate the transmission dynamics of pathogens in wildlife across the Arctic. Acknowledgments We thank the local subsistence hunters and communities in East Greenland, especially Jan Lorentzen, for ongoing collaboration and support with sample collection. We acknowledge Sandra Drewes Fabricius and Cecilie Nobel Zabel Dipo for their laboratory assistance. In addition, we thank Maria Jarque and Kim Hamonic for their assistance with sample transportation and permit acquisition. No animal care and use committee approvals were needed because samples were collected from deceased animals from the annual legal subsistence hunting quota of 35 Greenland polar bears. Polar bear samples were collected and transported to Denmark under the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora permits 16GL1166991, 17GL1167116, 18GL1717224, 19GL1717365, 20GL1717427, 21GL1717628, 22GL2089580 2022, 23GL2089714, 24GL2089884, 25GL2090110, IM 1202-580/16, IM 0818-549/17, IM 0928-712/18, IM0816-496/19, DK2020-0017113-01, DK-2021-0032841-01, DK-2022-0046312-01, DK-2023-0037644-01, DK-2024-0062523-01, DK-2025-0015153-01. Samples were transported to Norway and Canada under the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora permits DK-2025-0024770-01 and 26NO-0002-EX and Canadian Food Inspection Agency import permit A-2026-00277-1. We acknowledge Denmark’s Environmental Protection Agency for support through the Environmental Support for the Arctic program (Miljøstøtte til Arktis) and Cooperation for Environment in the Arctic (ZOO-PFAS grant no. 2022-86192 [awarded to C.S.], AMAP CORE BIOTA grant no. 2022-86218 [awarded to J.S.], and AMAP CORE BIOTA grant no. 2024-73867 [awarded to J.S.]). In addition, this work is funded by the European Union Horizon Europe (ArcSolution grant agreement no. 101135051), providing resources for the authors (C.S., R.D., and J.S.) to collect samples, and by the Morris Animal Foundation (grant no. D25ZO-430) and the Cornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Wildlife Health, providing early career support and funds for transportation and testing (awarded to K.J.B.). analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to detect antibodies to highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in East Greenland polar bears, addressing the emerging threat of HPAI in Arctic ecosystems. The research fills a knowledge gap by identifying HPAI exposure in polar bears, which are apex predators in the Arctic and may serve as sentinels for viral spread.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved collecting heart blood samples from 109 polar bears during the hunting season (January–May) from 2016 to 2025. Samples were collected from East Greenland and analyzed for antibodies against influenza A viruses using a competitive ELISA and hemagglutination inhibition assay.
analysis.methods: Samples were screened for antibodies against all influenza A viruses using a competitive ELISA, and further testing was conducted using a hemagglutination inhibition assay with avian influenza viruses representative of H5 and H7 subtypes. The study complied with international permits for sample collection and transport.
analysis.main_results: Three bears from 2024 and six bears from 2025 had antibodies to HPAI, with signal-to-noise values within the positive range. Four of the six 2025 bears had antibodies to the highly pathogenic H5 clade 2.3.4.4b, indicating recent exposure.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study provides evidence of HPAI exposure in East Greenland polar bears, highlighting the need for increased surveillance in Arctic ecosystems. The findings suggest that polar bears may serve as sentinels for HPAI spread and emphasize the importance of collaboration between scientists and local subsistence hunters.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings caution that HPAI may pose a risk to Arctic species, including polar bears, and underscore the need for enhanced surveillance and monitoring of viral spread in these regions. The study also highlights the strength of collaboration between scientists and local hunters in monitoring wildlife health.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the small sample size and the potential for cross-reactivity with low pathogenic H5 subtypes. However, the findings are supported by the high prevalence of antibodies and the survival of the bears post-exposure, suggesting a strong evidence base.

analysis.summary_en: This study detected antibodies to highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in East Greenland polar bears, indicating recent exposure. The findings highlight the need for increased surveillance in Arctic ecosystems and emphasize the importance of collaboration between scientists and local hunters.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在检测东格陵兰北极熊对高致病性禽流感(高致病性禽流感)的抗体,以应对高致病性禽流感对北极生态系统的新兴威胁。该研究通过识别北极熊对高致病性禽流感的暴露情况,填补了知识空白,北极熊作为北极地区的顶级捕食者,可能成为病毒传播的哨兵。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究涉及在2016年至2025年的狩猎季节(1月至5月)期间,从东格陵兰收集109只北极熊的心血样本,并使用竞争ELISA和血凝抑制试验检测这些样本中针对流感A病毒的抗体。
elements_zh.methods: 样本通过竞争ELISA检测针对所有流感A病毒的抗体,随后使用代表H5和H7亚型的禽流感病毒进行进一步的血凝抑制试验。本研究遵守了国际样本采集和运输许可。
elements_zh.main_results: 2024年的三只北极熊和2025年的六只北极熊对高致病性禽流感(HPAI)有抗体,信号与噪音比值处于阳性范围内。2025年的六只北极熊中有四只对高致病性H5亚型2.3.4.4b病毒有抗体,表明近期暴露。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 本研究提供了东格陵兰北极熊暴露于高致病性禽流感(HPAI)的证据,强调了在北极生态系统中增加监测监测的必要性。研究结果表明,北极熊可能作为HPAI传播的哨兵,并突显了科学家与当地生存狩猎者合作的重要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果警示高致病性禽流感(HPAI)可能对北极物种(包括北极熊)构成风险,并强调了在这些地区加强监测监测和病毒传播监控的必要性。此外,本研究还突显了科学家与当地狩猎者合作在监测野生动物健康方面的价值。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性在于样本量较小,以及可能与低致病性H5亚型发生交叉反应。然而,研究结果得到了抗体高患病率水平和北极熊暴露后存活的有力支持,表明其证据基础较强。}}.

papers.title: ATG13 Recruits LC3 to Target H9N2-IAV PB1 for Autophagic-Lysosomal Degradation and Restricts Viral Replication.
papers.abstract: Autophagy-related protein 13 (ATG13) is a critical component of the autophagy initiation complex and plays a pivotal role in regulating the initiation of autophagy. However, the precise mechanism by which ATG13 modulates influenza A virus (IAV) replication remains unclear. In this study, we demonstrated that ATG13 specifically interacts with the viral polymerase basic protein 1 (PB1) of H9N2-IAV and facilitates the autophagic degradation of PB1. Mechanistically, ATG13 targeted the C-terminal domain of PB1 and recruits microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 (LC3) to promote the autophagolysosomal degradation of PB1. This process counteracts the PB1-mediated degradation of mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS), thereby attenuating the immune evasion capacity of H9N2-IAV and ultimately suppressing viral replication. Collectively, our findings unveil for the first time a molecular mechanism whereby ATG13 negatively regulates IAV replication by mediating the targeted degradation of PB1 via the autophagolysosomal pathway. This study reveals a novel role of the autophagy pathway in host antiviral defense and provides a potential therapeutic target for anti-influenza agents.

papers.title_zh: ATG13通过自噬-溶酶体途径靶向H9N2-IAV PB1实现自噬降解并限制病毒复制
papers.source_body_en: Autophagy-related protein 13 (ATG13) is a critical component of the autophagy initiation complex and plays a pivotal role in regulating the initiation of autophagy. However, the precise mechanism by which ATG13 modulates influenza A virus (IAV) replication remains unclear. This process counteracts the PB1-mediated degradation of mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS), thereby attenuating the immune evasion capacity of H9N2-IAV and ultimately suppressing viral replication. papers.abstract_zh: 自噬相关蛋白13(ATG13)是自噬启动复合物的关键组分,其在调控自噬启动过程中起着核心作用。然而,ATG13如何精确调控流感病毒A(IAV)复制的机制尚不清楚。本研究中,我们证明ATG13特异性地与H9N2-IAV的病毒聚合酶基本蛋白1(PB1)相互作用,并促进PB1的自噬降解。机制上,ATG13靶向PB1的C端结构域,并招募微管相关蛋白1轻链3(LC3)以促进PB1的自噬-溶酶体降解。这一过程抵消了PB1介导的线粒体抗病毒信号蛋白(MAVS)的降解,从而削弱了H9N2-IAV的免疫逃逸能力,最终抑制病毒复制。综上所述,我们的研究首次揭示了ATG13通过自噬-溶酶体途径介导PB1的靶向降解,从而负向调控IAV复制的分子机制。本研究揭示了自噬途径在抗病毒防御中的新作用,并为抗流感药物提供了潜在的治疗靶点。

13:45 CET Virtual meeting Reading time: 2 min (532 words) Wednesday, 14 October 2026, 12:30 –13:45 (CEST) Background Avian influenza A(H9N2) viruses continue to circulate widely in birds and have caused sporadic human infections, highlighting the ongoing risk of influenza viruses emerging at the animal-human interface. Addressing these risks requires timely risk assessment, coordinated One Health action, across human, animal and environmental health sectors, and sustained preparedness for pandemics through GISRS and its partners. Held shortly after the WHO biannual consultation on influenza vaccine composition, including the review of candidate vaccine viruses for pandemic preparedness, this webinar will provide the latest updates on A(H9N2) epidemiology, virus characterization, animal and environmental surveillance, and global risk assessment. By bringing together experts from human, animal, and environmental health sectors, the webinar will promote a shared understanding of current risks and strengthen coordinated preparedness for future zoonotic and pandemic influenza threats. Objectives The webinar will provide a One Health update and support awareness on avian influenza A(H9N2) and provides an opportunity for engagement around the emerging Strategic Framework to accelerate Quadripartite action on avian influenza. Specific objectives are to: Summarize the current epidemiological situation of avian influenza A(H9N2) at the human–animal interface, including recent human infections and the geographical scope and impact of its spread in bird populations; Describe the virological characteristics of circulating A(H9N2) viruses and those detected in sporadic human cases, including antigenic and genetic diversity, markers of mammalian adaptation, and implications for risk assessment, diagnostics and candidate vaccine virus development; Highlight the roles of WHO, FAO, WOAH and UNEP in surveillance, risk assessment, prevention and control of avian influenza, including wildlife, poultry production, ecosystem and public health considerations; and Show how data and expertise from GISRS WHO Collaborating Centres and OFFLU contribute to global monitoring, virus characterization, risk assessment and preparedness for zoonotic and pandemic influenza threats. news.content_zh: 世界卫生组织(WHO)于2026年10月14日中午12:30至13:45(中欧时间)举办了题为'Understanding Influenza A(H9N2): current risks,One Health action and pandemic preparedness'的网络研讨会。该活动聚焦于持续在鸟类中广泛传播的禽流感 A(H9N2)病毒,该病毒已导致零星的人类感染。网络研讨会旨在通过及时的风险评估、跨人类、动物和环境健康领域的协调One Health行动以及持续的流行病预防准备,应对这些风险。该活动是在WHO关于流感疫苗组成的半年度咨询会议之后不久举行的,包括对用于流行病预防准备的候选疫苗病毒的审查。网络研讨会汇聚了来自不同领域的专家,以促进对当前风险的共同理解,并加强全球对未来人兽共患病和流行病流感威胁的准备。讨论内容包括A(H9N2)病毒的病毒学特征、其在鸟类种群中的传播情况,以及WHO、FAO、WOAH和UNEP在监测和预防中的作用。该活动是WHO健康紧急事件EPI-WIN计划的一部分,并强调了来自GISRS WHO合作中心和OFFLU的数据和专业知识在监测和准备工作中的重要性。

analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 网络研讨会提供了关于A(H9N2) 流行病学的最新信息,包括病毒特征分析和全球风险评估。其目标是通过WHO、FAO、WOAH和UNEP之间的合作,加强未来人兽共患病和流行病流感威胁的准备能力。

news.wechat_summary_zh: 时间：网络研讨会于2026年10月14日中午12：30至13：45(中欧时间)举行。活动日期为2026年10月14日，出版日期也为20...；地点与对象：该活动是由世界卫生组织(WHO)主办的虚拟会议。它汇集了来自全球人类、动物和环境健康领域的专家，重点关注禽流感 A(H9N2)及其对鸟类种群和零星人类感染的影响。；事件：WHO举办了题为'Understanding Influenza A(H9N2)： current risks，One Health action and pandemic preparedness'的网络研讨会，以讨论禽流感 A(H9N2)的持续...；影响与风险：禽流感 A(H9N2)病毒持续在鸟类中广泛传播，并导致零星的人类感染。网络研讨会强调了需要协调One Health行动和流行病预防准备，突出了流感病毒在动物-人类界面出现的持续风险。；应对与不确定性：网络研讨会提供了关于A(H9N2) 流行病学的最新信息，包括病毒特征分析和全球风险评估。其目标是通过WHO、FAO、WOAH和UNEP之间的合作，加强未来人兽共患病和流行病流感威胁的准备能力。

news.source_body_en: The Western Australian Government issued a notice on October 12, 2026, regarding H5 avian influenza, also known as bird flu. The notice highlights the importance of reporting cases and provides information about the virus. It does not specify exact case or death counts, nor does it detail health-system effects or operational impacts. The government is actively monitoring the situation and encouraging public awareness. The risk level is not explicitly stated in the notice. The content is a confirmed public health notice and does not include any information about testing, isolation, or prevention measures. The notice is part of ongoing efforts to manage and respond to avian influenza in the region.

analysis.location_and_population: Africa, specifically mentioning South Africa and Tanzania, with poultry and livestock populations at risk.
analysis.event: H5N1 bird flu has been reported to reach Africa, which is considered the last untouched continent, raising concerns about biosecurity. The report is from African Farming.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The article mentions the loss of 10 000 birds to bird flu and the culling of millions of birds, indicating significant impact on poultry populations. It also highlights the risk to jobs and the need for urgent vaccine measures.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The article discusses the need for improved biosecurity measures and mentions the culling of birds as a response. However, it does not provide details on testing, isolation, or contact tracing, leaving the response status uncertain.

analysis.brief_en: The article reports that H5N1 bird flu has reached Africa, which is regarded as the last untouched continent, serving as a chilling reminder about biosecurity. Published on October 15, 2026, by African Farming, the report highlights the impact of the virus on poultry populations, including the loss of 10,000 birds and the culling of millions. It emphasizes the risk to jobs and the urgent need for vaccine measures similar to those for foot-and-mouth disease. While the article discusses the importance of biosecurity and culling as a response, it does not provide specific details on testing, isolation, or contact tracing, leaving the response status uncertain. The report also mentions the broader implications for agriculture and farming communities across the continent.

news.title_zh: H5N1禽流感到达最后未触及的大陆——生物安全的‘警戒提醒’- 非洲农业
news.source_body_en: The article reports that H5N1 bird flu has reached Africa, which is regarded as the last untouched continent, serving as a chilling reminder about biosecurity. Published on October 15, 2026, by African Farming, the report highlights the impact of the virus on poultry populations, including the loss of 10,000 birds and the culling of millions. It emphasizes the risk to jobs and the urgent need for vaccine measures similar to those for foot-and-mouth disease. While the article discusses the importance of biosecurity and culling as a response, it does not provide specific details on testing, isolation, or contact tracing, leaving the response status uncertain. The report also mentions the broader implications for agriculture and farming communities across the continent.
news.content_zh: 文章报道,H5N1禽流感已到达非洲,被视为最后未触及的大陆,这提醒人们注意生物安全。该报告于2026年10月15日由非洲农业发布,强调了该病毒对家禽种群的影响,包括10,000只家禽死亡和数百万只家禽被扑杀。文章强调了对就业的影响以及迫切需要采取疫苗措施,类似于口蹄疫的防控措施。虽然文章讨论了生物安全和扑杀作为应对措施的重要性,但并未提供关于检测、隔离或接触追踪的具体细节,因此应对措施的状态尚不确定。报告还提到了该病毒对非洲农业和农民社区的更广泛影响。

news.content: ___ × Market Information Top Poultry Companies Expert Insights Blogs Regions Magazines Sign In Poultry Meat Egg Poultry Health Sustainability Poultry Future Chicken Marketing Summit Poultry Tech Summit Broilers & Turkeys Diseases & Health Avian Influenza Avian influenza strikes Peruvian laying hen flock Approximately half of the birds in a flock of 5,800 died prior to culling activities. Roy Graber October 14, 2026 Article Summary Highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 was confirmed in a Peruvian laying hen flock in October, killing nearly 3,000 birds and forcing the depopulation of the remaining 2,860 hens, just over a month after the country had been declared free of the virus. H5N1 HPAI confirmed on October 7 in Centro Poblado El Tallán, Peru affecting a commercial laying hen flock 5,800 hens total: 2,940 died from infection and 2,860 were depopulated to control spread Infected birds showed respiratory and neurological signs before confirmation Outbreak occurred just over one month after Peru was declared H5N1-free on September 3 Response included quarantine measures, facility disinfection, and surveillance around the outbreak area Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) has been confirmed in a commercial laying hen flock in Centro Poblado El Tallán, Peru. According to a report from the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), the case was confirmed Oct. 7. Of the 5,800 hens in the flock, 2,940 died and the remaining 2,860 were depopulated, the report said. The hens had exhibited respiratory and neurological signs. Once an H5N1 variant of HPAI was confirmed, the birds were stamped out, quarantine measures were taken and an epidemiological investigation was launched. Healthy Living Washington Confirms Its First H5N1 Bird Flu Cases in Dairy Cattle, Placing Two Yakima County Farms Under Quarantine Published Oct 09, 2026 10:48 PM EDT By Dorothy Brooks Cole Burston | Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket Washington has confirmed its first known cases of H5N1 bird flu in dairy cattle. Two dairy farms in Yakima County are now under quarantine after federal laboratory testing confirmed the virus, the Washington State Department of Agriculture announced Thursday. The detection ends a long run of negative results. State officials said more than 7,000 surveillance tests for the virus over the past two years had all come back negative. According to the department, dairy cattle in 19 states have been infected since the national outbreak began in March 2024. For most households, the immediate risk is low and pasteurized milk remains safe. The greater concern falls on farmworkers, dairy families, veterinarians and anyone in the region who drinks raw milk or gives raw dairy to pets. Two Quarantined Farms and Two Years of Negative Tests According to the state agriculture department's announcement, the virus was detected by the Washington Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory at Washington State University and confirmed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture's National Veterinary Services Laboratories. Both farms are quarantined and have put strict biosecurity measures in place. State staff are carrying out on-farm investigations and additional testing, and veterinarians are treating sick cows. Officials said most affected cattle recover with supportive care, typically within about six weeks. The department did not say how the virus reached the herds. It noted that wild birds can carry the virus but are not considered the main source of spread between dairy herds. Infected animals, contaminated milk, and equipment, vehicles or people moving between farms are the main routes. "We appreciate how difficult this is for our dairy families, farmworkers and veterinarians," said Dr. Amber Itle, Washington's state veterinarian. Capital Press reported the same core details. The agriculture department said it will issue a news release for each newly affected county, while later detections in counties already announced will be posted online. Washington's Place in a National Dairy Outbreak The Yakima County detections add a major Pacific Northwest dairy state to a national outbreak that began in March 2024. MedicalDaily previously reported that more than 1,166 dairy herds across 19 states had been affected as of late July, based on USDA data, with Idaho leading the nation. A current national herd total could not be confirmed at publication because the USDA livestock detections pagedisplays its figures in an interactive dashboard. Readers can check that page for updated counts. Human infections remain uncommon. The CDC's bird flu situation summary lists 71 human H5 cases in the United States since 2024, as of its last update in March, and says the current public health risk is low. Officials did not report any human cases tied to the Yakima County herds. Washington's earlier human cases, reported in 2024, involved workers handling infected poultry at a commercial egg farm in Franklin County. H5N1 has circulated in Washington birds since 2022. The dairy detection adds a new animal population for officials to monitor, along with the workers and families who care for those animals every day. Milk Safety, Raw Dairy and Farmworker Precautions State officials said pasteurized milk and dairy products remain safe and that milk shortages are not expected. Pasteurization inactivates the virus. Raw milk is a different matter. Infected cows can shed the virus in their milk, and the agriculture department says raw milk and raw dairy products are unsafe. The Washington State Department of Health warns that raw milk is never a guaranteed safe product because it lacks the protection of pasteurization. The agriculture department also advises against giving pets raw milk, other raw dairy or raw foods. People who work closely with dairy cattle, poultry or other potentially infected animals face the highest risk. The agriculture department calls for gloves, masks, eye protection and fluid-resistant coveralls when working with sick animals or raw milk. State health department guidance for agricultural workers goes further, recommending safety goggles, an N95 respirator or better, and rubber boots. Workers who develop eye redness, cough, fever or other flu-like symptoms after animal contact should call a health care provider and mention the exposure. Dairy producers are urged to watch their herds closely. Warning signs include thicker milk that is often yellowish to brown, lower milk production, reduced feed intake, fever, respiratory signs, changes in manure and a sharp drop in rumination. Itle urged producers to strengthen biosecurity and report signs of illness right away. The agriculture department's animal health team can be reached at 360-902-1878. Testing, Reporting and the Next Updates Officials have not said whether more herds in Yakima County or elsewhere in Washington are being tested as part of the response. Any detection in a new county would trigger a new public announcement. The agency recommends isolating newly arriving animals for 30 days, keeping milk from sick cows out of the bulk tank, separating sick cattle and avoiding shared equipment or workers between farms. Because wild birds are not the main route between herds, farm-level precautions carry much of the burden of prevention. For families in the Yakima Valley and across Washington, the practical steps are specific. Choose pasteurized milk and dairy, keep raw milk away from children and pets, and report sick or dead animals to state officials rather than handling them. Farmworkers with symptoms after cattle contact should seek prompt medical advice. MedicalDaily will follow updates from Washington agriculture and health officials, as well as federal herd counts from USDA. The central open questions are how the virus entered these two herds and whether more Washington farms are affected. The state agriculture department confirmed H5N1 bird flu in dairy cattle at two Yakima County farms. It is the first known detection in Washington cattle. Are the farms under quarantine? Yes. Both farms are quarantined and have added strict biosecurity measures, and veterinarians are treating sick cows. Is store-bought milk safe to drink? Yes. State officials said pasteurized milk and dairy products remain safe and no milk shortages are expected. Pasteurization inactivates the virus. Is raw milk risky? Yes. Infected cows can shed the virus in milk, and state officials say raw milk and raw dairy are unsafe for people and should not be given to pets. Have any people been infected from these herds? Officials did not report any human cases linked to the Yakima County herds. CDC considers the overall public health risk low. Who should take extra precautions? Dairy and poultry workers, veterinarians and others in close contact with sick animals should wear protective gear and report symptoms such as eye redness or fever. Healthy Living Washington Confirms Its First H5N1 Bird Flu Cases in Dairy Cattle, Placing Two Yakima County Farms Under Quarantine Published Oct 09, 2026 10:48 PM EDT By Dorothy Brooks Cole Burston | Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket Washington has confirmed its first known cases of H5N1 bird flu in dairy cattle. Two dairy farms in Yakima County are now under quarantine after federal laboratory testing confirmed the virus, the Washington State Department of Agriculture announced Thursday. The detection ends a long run of negative results. State officials said more than 7,000 surveillance tests for the virus over the past two years had all come back negative. According to the department, dairy cattle in 19 states have been infected since the national outbreak began in March 2024. For most households, the immediate risk is low and pasteurized milk remains safe. The greater concern falls on farmworkers, dairy families, veterinarians and anyone in the region who drinks raw milk or gives raw dairy to pets. Two Quarantined Farms and Two Years of Negative Tests According to the state agriculture department's announcement, the virus was detected by the Washington Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory at Washington State University and confirmed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture's National Veterinary Services Laboratories. Both farms are quarantined and have put strict biosecurity measures in place. State staff are carrying out on-farm investigations and additional testing, and veterinarians are treating sick cows. Officials said most affected cattle recover with supportive care, typically within about six weeks. The department did not say how the virus reached the herds. It noted that wild birds can carry the virus but are not considered the main source of spread between dairy herds. Infected animals, contaminated milk, and equipment, vehicles or people moving between farms are the main routes. "We appreciate how difficult this is for our dairy families, farmworkers and veterinarians," said Dr. Amber Itle, Washington's state veterinarian. Capital Press reported the same core details. The agriculture department said it will issue a news release for each newly affected county, while later detections in counties already announced will be posted online. Washington's Place in a National Dairy Outbreak The Yakima County detections add a major Pacific Northwest dairy state to a national outbreak that began in March 2024. MedicalDaily previously reported that more than 1,166 dairy herds across 19 states had been affected as of late July, based on USDA data, with Idaho leading the nation. A current national herd total could not be confirmed at publication because the USDA livestock detections pagedisplays its figures in an interactive dashboard. Readers can check that page for updated counts. Human infections remain uncommon. The CDC's bird flu situation summary lists 71 human H5 cases in the United States since 2024, as of its last update in March, and says the current public health risk is low. Officials did not report any human cases tied to the Yakima County herds. Washington's earlier human cases, reported in 2024, involved workers handling infected poultry at a commercial egg farm in Franklin County. H5N1 has circulated in Washington birds since 2022. The dairy detection adds a new animal population for officials to monitor, along with the workers and families who care for those animals every day. Milk Safety, Raw Dairy and Farmworker Precautions State officials said pasteurized milk and dairy products remain safe and that milk shortages are not expected. Pasteurization inactivates the virus. Raw milk is a different matter. Infected cows can shed the virus in their milk, and the agriculture department says raw milk and raw dairy products are unsafe. The Washington State Department of Health warns that raw milk is never a guaranteed safe product because it lacks the protection of pasteurization. The agriculture department also advises against giving pets raw milk, other raw dairy or raw foods. People who work closely with dairy cattle, poultry or other potentially infected animals face the highest risk. The agriculture department calls for gloves, masks, eye protection and fluid-resistant coveralls when working with sick animals or raw milk. State health department guidance for agricultural workers goes further, recommending safety goggles, an N95 respirator or better, and rubber boots. Workers who develop eye redness, cough, fever or other flu-like symptoms after animal contact should call a health care provider and mention the exposure. Dairy producers are urged to watch their herds closely. Warning signs include thicker milk that is often yellowish to brown, lower milk production, reduced feed intake, fever, respiratory signs, changes in manure and a sharp drop in rumination. Itle urged producers to strengthen biosecurity and report signs of illness right away. The agriculture department's animal health team can be reached at 360-902-1878. Testing, Reporting and the Next Updates Officials have not said whether more herds in Yakima County or elsewhere in Washington are being tested as part of the response. Any detection in a new county would trigger a new public announcement. The agency recommends isolating newly arriving animals for 30 days, keeping milk from sick cows out of the bulk tank, separating sick cattle and avoiding shared equipment or workers between farms. Because wild birds are not the main route between herds, farm-level precautions carry much of the burden of prevention. For families in the Yakima Valley and across Washington, the practical steps are specific. Choose pasteurized milk and dairy, keep raw milk away from children and pets, and report sick or dead animals to state officials rather than handling them. Farmworkers with symptoms after cattle contact should seek prompt medical advice. MedicalDaily will follow updates from Washington agriculture and health officials, as well as federal herd counts from USDA. The central open questions are how the virus entered these two herds and whether more Washington farms are affected. Both farms are quarantined and have added strict biosecurity measures, and veterinarians are treating sick cows. Is store-bought milk safe to drink? Yes. State officials said pasteurized milk and dairy products remain safe and no milk shortages are expected. Pasteurization inactivates the virus. Is raw milk risky? Yes. Infected cows can shed the virus in milk, and state officials say raw milk and raw dairy are unsafe for people and should not be given to pets. Have any people been infected from these herds? Officials did not report any human cases linked to the Yakima County herds. CDC considers the overall public health risk low. Who should take extra precautions? Dairy and poultry workers, veterinarians and others in close contact with sick animals should wear protective gear and report symptoms such as eye redness or fever. supplementary_news.content: The sweeter side of veterinary medicine Welcome to your new favorite place to grow in vet med. Discover brilliant experts, engaging videos, interactive quizzes, inspiring stories, and podcasts that keep you curious, connected, and excited about what's next. After serving in the U.S. Navy, raising a family while earning her veterinary degree, and drawing inspiration from her immigrant mother's entrepreneurial journey, Dr. Lieu Balu is preparing to lead her own veterinary clinic in Phoenix. Scientists detect H5 bird flu antibodies in apparently healthy Greenland polar bears, raising new concerns about wildlife disease spread in the Arctic. Ask most people what a veterinary pathologist does all day and they’ll probably picture microscopes, slides, cells, and very serious diagnostic reports. Dr. Aleksandra Zuraw certainly does all of that. New research involving nearly 900 dogs reveals that larger breeds don't just have shorter lives. Their bodies may actually age faster at the molecular level, and the discovery could change how scientists approach canine longevity. H5N1 bird flu strikes Minnesota turkey and Indiana duck farms as another Texas dairy herd tests positive, raising new concerns for veterinarians. LMU researchers challenge a decades-old model: genetically modified embryos lacking interferon tau can establish pregnancies and develop into healthy calves. A landmark Purina study found that lean Labrador Retrievers lived 1.8 years longer and developed chronic disease later. Here's why the findings still matter for veterinarians 25 years later. Scientists warn that emerging African swine fever variants could undermine vaccine protection, making surveillance and biosecurity more important than ever. Letter of Reasonable Assurance clears the way for Maryland’s first in-state veterinary school to begin recruiting and admitting its inaugural class in 2027 11 careers. 6 questions. Zero chill. Veterinary medicine isn't one job—it's about eleven careers hiding under the same white coat. There is a conversation happening in break rooms, group chats, and parking lots all over veterinary medicine. It usually starts the same way. I love the medicine, but I do not know how much longer I can do this. And it usually ends with a quiet assumption that something is wrong with the person saying it. Somewhere along the way, veterinary medicine developed an unwritten rule: clinical practice is the real job, and everything else is quitting. It gets absorbed in school, reinforced in practice, and carried around as guilt by veterinarians who are exhausted, curious, or simply ready for a change but afraid that stepping out of the exam room means abandoning their oath. If you are graduating this year, the offers are probably already arriving, and some of the numbers are eye-watering. Signing bonuses have become the headline of new grad recruitment, and with student debt where it is, nobody could blame you for reading the biggest number and reaching for a pen. Vet school can turn almost anything into a performance metric. Grades, class rank, clinical skills, productivity, sleep, exercise, and sometimes even food can quietly become one more thing you feel like you should be “doing right.” Add long days, irregular schedules, stress, limited money, constant comparison, and a culture that can reward pushing through discomfort, and it is easy for a complicated relationship with food or your body to hide in plain sight. There are queer and trans veterinarians who came before you, students at other schools experiencing many of the same things, peer-support volunteers willing to listen, community organizations that know your city, and national groups that can help when a problem becomes medical, legal, academic, or overwhelming. Vet school has a way of eating your entire calendar. Between exams, labs, rotations, boards, jobs, relationships, and trying to get enough sleep to remain functional, personal health can slide down the priority list pretty quickly. There is a particular kind of kitchen alchemy that happens when nothing gets thrown away: a roast chicken becomes dinner, then lunch, then the broth for Thursday's ramen. A single Sunday afternoon becomes a month of breakfasts. What follows is not a diet plan so much as a system, one built on a $500 monthly grocery budget, a single person's appetite, and the stubborn belief that homemade is both cheaper and better. Meet Mecca Gladney, a first-generation college graduate, mother, and University of Arizona veterinary student pursuing a career in veterinary surgery while championing representation, mentorship, and mental health. The UC Davis veterinary student took a winding road to her dream school, but every setback helped shape the veterinarian and mentor she hopes to become. Now Monika Lagarejos wants to use her place in veterinary medicine to care for animals, strengthen communities, and make sure the next generation of future veterinarians knows they belong. McPaul Hermoso started veterinary school at 35 after earning multiple degrees and living in five countries. Discover his unconventional journey, lifelong dream of becoming a veterinarian, and mission to inspire others. From four years cheering at LSU to studying veterinary medicine at the Royal Veterinary College, Jalyne Blackwell is building a career by saying yes to the opportunities that scare her a little—and trusting that the unexpected path might be the right one. After France’s competitive exams shut the door, this 20-year-old found her calling 800 miles from home — and proof that a detour can still lead exactly where you were meant to go. Meet Taja Bell, an LSU veterinary student, Army Animal Care Specialist, mom and model working toward a future in emergency medicine and surgery. There is a particular kind of courage it takes to walk away from a career you have already proven yourself in and start over as a first-year student. Emese Avdeyenkova has done exactly that, twice over, once when she traded a biology degree for an Army uniform, and again when she traded that uniform for a white coat. Now she is bringing all of it, the discipline, the humility, and the hard-won perspective, to Vet Candy Radio as one of the vet student hosts of Vet School After Dark. America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer and her cat daddy husband Clay Palmer dig into the real science, history, and psychology behind humanity's longest-running obsession. We're talking ancient Egypt, where cats were literally worshipped as gods. We're talking the internet, where cats generate more content than almost anything else on the planet. From ancient worship to TikTok stardom, cats have clawed their way into our hearts and honestly, they never asked for permission. But why? What is it about the most indifferent creature on the planet that makes humans absolutely lose their minds? Think black cats bring bad luck? Think again. The truth about black cats is stranger, richer, and way more interesting than the superstition and Caitlin and Clay are here to set the record straight. In this episode of Cat Cafe, America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer and her cat daddy husband Clay Palmer dive deep into the wild world of cat mythology, feline folklore, and the weirdest cat superstitions that humans have carried for centuries. We are talking black cats across cultures — feared in some, worshipped in others. We are talking mythological cats from ancient Egypt to Norse legends to the shadowy corners of the internet. We are talking the real history behind the myths that still follow these animals into shelters today, where black cats consistently wait the longest for homes. Spoiler: the cats were never the problem. Think you know everything about cats? In this hilarious episode of Cat Cafe, America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer takes on the ultimate cat trivia challenge — and her cat daddy husband Clay is putting her knowledge to the test. From quirky cat facts to surprising feline science, this quiz will challenge even the most devoted cat lovers. Play along and see if you can beat America’s favorite veterinary receptionist, Caitlin Palmer! But it's not just fun and games. Every wrong answer comes with a punishment — and that punishment is pickle juice. Yes, really. Watch to find out who walks away victorious and who walks away regretting their cat knowledge gaps. • Fun (and tricky) cat trivia questions • Surprising cat facts you probably didn’t know • A very questionable pickle juice challenge Who’s the ultimate cat nerd... and who’s about to drink pickle juice? In this hilarious episode of Pet Candy, Caitlin and Clay go head-to-head in a cat trivia challenge with a twist—get a question wrong, and you have to take a sip of pickle juice Think you know cats? Play along and see if you can beat them (without the punishment.) Every NAVLE Warrior asks some version of the same question during week six: am I studying the right way, or am I just studying the most? Cognitive science has a real answer to that question, and it is not the one most students expect Every NAVLE study plan is built around content: which species, which systems, which diagnoses to drill. But the brain that has to hold all of that information is a physical organ, and it runs on three inputs: sleep, movement, and nutrition. Neglect any one of them and the same number of practice questions will produce worse results. Here's the science behind why, and what to actually do about it. Starting with the October to November 2026 testing window, the NAVLE looks different in two ways that actually matter for how you study. The exam moved to a new block format back in the spring update, and now the ICVA has also refreshed the Species and Diagnosis list itself, adding more than 100 diseases across the species you'll be tested on. That is not a small revision. That is the blueprint growing, and it means the way you have been prepping needs a second look. Paid NAVLE prep services can cost more than $600 for a thirty month pass, sometimes more. For companies selling them, that is a subscription. For a fourth-year veterinary student, that can be groceries for two months. And in a year when gas prices and food prices have squeezed every budget in America, plenty of vet students are doing math far scarier than anything on the exam. There are continuing education programs, and then there are continuing education programs where you accidentally debunk a mythical creature between bites of fried dough. This particular offering from Vet Candy lands firmly in the second category. Based on a short story by Vet Candy’s CEO and X-Files super fan, Dr. Jill Lopez. Dr. Joya Griffin and Dr. Forrest Cummings just dropped the veterinary CE series that changes how you think about complex cases and it is free with your Vet Candy membership. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Unleash Your Inner Hero! , an 8-module urgent care program led by veterinary criticalist Dr. Natosha Richardson. Offering 3.5 RACE CE credits for veterinarians and veterinary technicians, this course covers triage, CPR, supportive care, diagnostics, and treatment across neurologic, gastrointestinal, respiratory, and integumentary emergencies. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Dermatology Secrets featuring Dr. Joya Griffin. This three-part online course is designed for veterinarians and veterinary technicians and covers the dermatology skills that matter most in everyday practice — skin cytology, histopathology and biopsy interpretation, and the strangest and most diagnostically challenging cases in specialist dermatology. Learn how to read a cytology slide with confidence, decode a dermatopathology report, and work through complex skin presentations that have not responded to standard treatment. Earn 1.5 RACE CE credits at no cost with your free Vet Candy Membership! Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with the Respiratory Disease Master Course featuring Criticalist Dr. Anthony Gonzalez. Brought to you by Trudell Animal Health, this 8-module course provides 4 RACE CE credits for veterinarians and veterinary technicians. It covers recognition, diagnosis, and management of acute and chronic respiratory disease, including practical guidance on critical care, advanced monitoring, oxygen therapy, and evidence-based treatment strategies. Designed for immediate clinical application, this course helps veterinary professionals improve outcomes in high-stakes respiratory cases. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Endocrinology Secrets featuring Dr. Forrest Cummings. This online course is designed for veterinarians and veterinary technicians and covers real-world management of diabetes in dogs and cats, Cushing’s disease, and Addison’s disease. Learn how to interpret diagnostics, manage challenging endocrine cases, and improve patient outcomes with practical, case-based guidance. Earn 2 RACE CE credits at no cost—no subscription or credit card required. The Gut-Brain connection is more connected than we thought. This episode of Catching Up explores the fascinating link between the gut and brain in pets. Could your patient's GI issues be tied to behavior? The science says yes. Acute Kidney Injury Alert: New Biomarkers That Could Save Lives. Dr. Elan Armstrong & Dr. Shannon Gregoire break down the newest research on acute kidney injury. World-First Breakthrough: Stem Cells from Cats Could Revolutionize Kidney Disease Treatment! Vet Candy has the details with Dr. Elan & Dr. Shannon. Big news in hemangiosarcoma research! Tune in as we cover a promising breakthrough that could change the way we approach this aggressive cancer. Inside: Dr. Wailani Sung helps you learn how to Recognize the Subtle Signs of Pain in Cats. Presented by Zoetis, maker of Solensia. SolensiaVetTeam.com A cat eye that won't heal is one of those cases that can quietly spiral into something serious — fast. In this episode of Rounds with Dr. Shannon, Dr. Shannon Gregoire sits down with veterinary ophthalmologist Dr. DJ Haeussler for a real clinical conversation about the feline eye cases that challenge general practitioners the most, starting with the corneal ulcer that just won't close. A limping dog walks into your exam room. The owner says it started two weeks ago. The leg looks fine. The X-rays look fine. Nothing adds up — yet. In this episode of Mystery Case Rounds, Dr. Shannon Gregoire walks through a real clinical case of canine lameness from the first exam to the final diagnosis, showing exactly how she thinks through a case when the answer isn't obvious. Veterinary emergency specialist Dr. Kristin Welch walks through a real hyperglycemia case that didn't follow the textbook. Watch the diagnostic reasoning unfold on Vet Candy's Mystery Case Rounds. Dr. Ashley Bourgeois breaks down what is really going on when a Pomeranian loses its coat, the hormonal, genetic, and inflammatory factors may be at play, why this breed is uniquely predisposed to certain dermatologic conditions, and how to build a workup that actually leads somewhere instead of chasing your tail. Nearly a quarter of homeless youth in the U.S. have pets — and some choose veterinary care over their own health care. The Seattle One Health Clinic offers both, side by side, for free. Jeremiah Pouncy shares why this One Health model is changing how we think about the human-animal bond and community care. In Barcelona, scientists are building a biological deep freeze for endangered species, storing genetic material from nearly 300 species and using AI to unlock the future of conservation. Jeremiah Pouncy explains how the Barcelona CryoZoo could change everything we know about saving wildlife from extinction. With fewer than 800 left on Earth, the Bengal florican is one of the rarest birds alive. But in India's Manas National Park, over 800 former poachers have become the species' fiercest protectors. Jeremiah Pouncy tells the remarkable story of how community-led conservation turned a near-extinction into a comeback. A new study on the "Capitoline dolphins" off Rome's coast reveals a population in crisis. Seven out of ten show signs of malnutrition, many bear scars from fishing gear, and scientists warn they may disappear without urgent intervention. Jeremiah Pouncy breaks down what is threatening one of the world's most historically significant dolphin populations and why it matters. Going back to veterinary school usually means new classes, new rotations, new schedules, and the familiar feeling that summer disappeared way too fast. For the hosts of Vet School After Dark , it also means catching up on where everyone spent the break and figuring out how to mentally transition back into another demanding academic year. Vet Candy's hit podcast recently went live in Nashville, and what started as another fast-paced battle of veterinary knowledge quickly turned into something no one in the room saw coming. Dr. Lauren Downey Koos didn't have to look far to get to WVC Nashville. She works at BluePearl Veterinary in Franklin, Tennessee, which means the conference is essentially in her backyard. She graduated from the University of Florida in 2018, went into neurology, and became a specialist faster than most people finish paying off their student loans. Hosts Caitlin and Clay Palmer, the masterminds behind Vet Candy's trivia and news game show, challenge Carey to a fast-paced reckoning with the week's wildest veterinary headlines, most surprising research breakthroughs, and oddest animal stories circulating through the profession. It's loosely inspired by NPR's Wait Wait... Don't Tell Me, except everyone involved actually knows what a splenectomy is. Veterinary technicians Peter Carlos and Jaycee join Vet Candy's Medical Mysteries to tell the story of a cat with an acutely enlarged abdomen and a diagnosis nobody saw coming. Read Vet Candy's fr…

supplementary_news.content: ___ Market Information Top Poultry Companies Expert Insights Blogs Regions Magazines Sign In Poultry Meat Egg Poultry Health Sustainability Poultry Future Chicken Marketing Summit Poultry Tech Summit Broilers & Turkeys Diseases & Health Avian Influenza Avian influenza strikes Peruvian laying hen flock Approximately half of the birds in a flock of 5,800 died prior to culling activities. Roy Graber October 14, 2026 Article Summary Highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 was confirmed in a Peruvian laying hen flock in October, killing nearly 3,000 birds and forcing the depopulation of the remaining 2,860 hens, just over a month after the country had been declared free of the virus. H5N1 HPAI confirmed on October 7 in Centro Poblado El Tallán, Peru affecting a commercial laying hen flock 5,800 hens total: 2,940 died from infection and 2,860 were depopulated to control spread Infected birds showed respiratory and neurological signs before confirmation Outbreak occurred just over one month after Peru was declared H5N1-free on September 3 Response included quarantine measures, facility disinfection, and surveillance around the outbreak area Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) has been confirmed in a commercial laying hen flock in Centro Poblado El Tallán, Peru. According to a report from the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), the case was confirmed Oct. 7. Of the 5,800 hens in the flock, 2,940 died and the remaining 2,860 were depopulated, the report said. The hens had exhibited respiratory and neurological signs. Once an H5N1 variant of HPAI was confirmed, the birds were stamped out, quarantine measures were taken and an epidemiological investigation was launched. The epidemiological unit was cleaned and disinfected, and surveillance was conducted around the outbreak to detect possible cases, WOAH said. The infection came just over a month after Peruvian poultry was declared free of H5N1 HPAI. The previous outbreak was resolved Sept. 3. WOAH also has active reports on HPAI in nonpoultry and wild birds in Peru, including one concerning the H5N1 subtype and another concerning an untyped H5 HPAI variant. WOAH has an active report on Newcastle disease in Peru as well, but that report has not been updated in more than a month. View our continuing coverage of the global avian influenza situation. Edited by: Damián Morais State agriculture officials quarantine two commercial dairies in Yakima County following the Pacific Northwest state’s first confirmed detections of H5N1 in cattle. The Washington State Department of Agriculture (WSDA) and the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) National Veterinary Services Laboratories have confirmed the state’s first cases of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) H5N1 in dairy cattle, placing two commercial dairy operations in Yakima County under mandatory quarantine. The confirmed detections expand the geographic reach of the bovine influenza outbreak, making Washington the twentieth U.S. state to identify H5N1 in dairy cattle since the cross-species transmission was first documented in early 2024. State and local health authorities, including the Yakima Health District, have activated clinical surveillance protocols to monitor exposed dairy workers and veterinary personnel. Public health officials emphasize that while human transmission risks remain low and pasteurized commercial milk supplies remain safe, immediate movement restrictions and enhanced biosecurity barriers are mandatory to contain localized spread. See also: Fonterra’s 25-year milk price legacy shaped by global market dynamics From an animal pathology and veterinary perspective, H5N1 manifestation in lactating dairy cattle presents a distinct clinical profile compared to the acute mortality observed in avian species. Affected cows typically exhibit sudden lethargy, diminished dry-matter feed intake, ruminal stasis, and a precipitous decline in daily milk yield. The raw milk produced by infected animals undergoes marked physical changes, turning into a thickened, yellow, colostrum-like secretion characterized by elevated somatic cell counts and high viral loads shed directly from mammary epithelial tissue. While mortality among adult cows remains low—with most animals regaining baseline health and partial lactation persistency over a two-to-three-week supportive therapy regimen—the disease inflicts temporary metabolic distress and significant milk solids losses. State veterinarians are requiring affected herds to isolate clinical animals, restrict milk disposal to prevent wildlife scavenging, and divert affected secretions away from the bulk tank. From a food safety and commercial processing standpoint, the confirmation of H5N1 within Washington’s raw milk shed does not compromise the commercial retail supply chain. Federal regulatory agencies, including the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the USDA, have repeatedly validated that commercial thermal pasteurization—whether High-Temperature Short-Time (HTST) or Higher-Heat Shorter-Time (HHST)—effectively inactivates influenza viruses, rendering store-bought fluid milk, cheese, and cultured products completely safe for human consumption. However, the presence of active viral shedding represents an acute health hazard for unpasteurized dairy consumption. Agricultural authorities have reissued strict public health warnings emphasizing that raw milk or unpasteurized dairy products derived from infected or unmonitored herds are unsafe for human or domestic animal consumption, highlighting that raw milk ingestion has historically driven fatal viral transmissions in farm cats and companion animals. The Yakima County detections introduce heightened operational and logistical friction across the Pacific Northwest dairy corridor, an intensive milk shed closely interconnected with neighboring Idaho and Oregon. Dairy co-operatives and private hauling operators must enforce rigorous sanitation protocols across bulk milk transport tankers, intake docks, and receiving bays to eliminate mechanical vector transfer between production sites. Furthermore, under federal animal health orders, producers transporting lactating dairy cows across state lines must conduct pre-movement testing through approved National Animal Health Laboratory Network (NAHLN) facilities. For farm managers, safeguarding production units requires implementing closed-herd protocols, restricting non-essential visitor access, establishing vehicle disinfection wheel baths, and equipping milking parlor personnel with personal protective equipment (PPE)—including eye protection, masks, and gloves—to prevent aerosol transmission during high-pressure parlor washdowns. See also: Western Star marks centenary with leading position in Australian butter market At the farmgate level, H5N1 quarantines impose direct balance sheet stress on commercial dairy operations. The combination of immediate milk yield losses, veterinary care expenditures, testing fees, and isolated disposal logistics quickly compresses operating margins. Although federal risk-mitigation programs—such as the USDA’s Emergency Assistance for Livestock, Honeybees, and Farm-Raised Fish Program (ELAP) and financial assistance for biosecurity implementation—provide partial indemnities for lost milk production and testing expenses, operational cash flows face disruption during quarantine periods. Sustaining disciplined biosecurity compliance and collaborating with state veterinary services will be critical for Pacific Northwest producers seeking to resolve active herd infections, lift quarantine orders, and protect herd asset value heading into 2027. Play/PauseSPACE Increase Volume↑ Decrease Volume↓ Seek Forward→ Seek Backward← Captions On/Offc Fullscreen/Exit Fullscreenf Mute/Unmutem Decrease Caption Size- Increase Caption Size+ or = Seek %0-9 Auto360p1080p720p540p360p270p180p Live 00:00 01:41 01:41 WASHINGTON, D.C. (RFD-TV) — The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) is urging poultry and livestock producers to stay vigilant against highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) as fall bird migration begins. Cases declined during the summer months, but the seasonal movement of wild birds raises renewed concerns about the virus’s spread. USDA Under Secretary of Marketing & Regulatory Programs Dudley Hoskins says basic biosecurity practices remain essential to reducing transmission risks at agricultural facilities. “Think about clothing, think about your footwear, where you’ve been, washing your hands, what facility you may have been at that morning versus where you may be going that afternoon,” Hoskins said. “Anything you can do just to maintain vigilance and awareness of those kinds of fundamental principles is really what we’re asking people to do.” While poultry remains a primary concern, cattle producers are also monitoring the virus because dairy cattle are susceptible to HPAI. Hoskins says education and prevention efforts need to extend beyond farm operations. USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service is working to mitigate the virus’s impact on American agriculture and producers. Hoskins says producers can help by educating employees, visitors, and people outside the farm gate about biosecurity practices. The current HPAI outbreak began in early 2022. USDA reports that approximately 31 million birds have been culled as part of the response. That figure does not mean every bird was confirmed to be infected, as depopulation may include birds exposed to the virus as part of disease-control efforts.
