One possible genetic clue is clade 2.3.2.1a, which was identified in poultry samples from the state in 2024. It was also detected in the virus that killed a two-year-old girl from Palnadu district in March 2025.Andhra Pradesh recorded two bird flu outbreak epicentres in February 2024, leading to the culling of about 300 birds. The scale increased sharply in 2025, when eight epicentres were reported across the state. More than 5.4 lakh birds died or were culled during those outbreaks in 2025.An older viral lineage:The National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD) identified clade 2.3.2.1a in poultry samples collected in Andhra Pradesh in 2024. At a World Organisation for Animal Health workshop in South Korea in August 2024, NIHSAD presented findings linking the samples to a lineage that has circulated in South Asia for several years.The same clade was identified in the virus detected in the Palnadu child. An H5N1 infection in an 11-year-old boy in Haryana in 2021 was also linked to this lineage. Research has additionally documented a human infection involving the broader clade 2.3.2.1 group in Nepal in 2019. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like Leave Some Honey Out For Your Dog Overnight, Here’s What HappensPets Daily Health Learn More Undo Genetic comparisons have shown similarities between viruses detected in India and Bangladesh, where clade 2.3.2.1a has circulated or re-emerged in poultry and other birds.A complex genetic history:The ICMR-National Institute of Virology in Pune analysed the Palnadu child’s specimen and submitted the genetic data to the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data (GISAID). The sequence belonged to clade 2.3.2.1a and clustered with a virus associated with an H5N1 infection reported in a child who fell ill while visiting Kolkata in 2024 and was diagnosed after returning to Australia.A study published in ‘Emerging Infectious Diseases’ found that the Australian virus was a reassortant, meaning its genome contained segments derived from different influenza virus lineages. Four gene segments, including the haemagglutinin segment, were most closely related to clade 2.3.2.1a viruses circulating in Bangladesh. Other segments showed relationships to viruses detected in Japan, South Korea and China, as well as to a low-pathogenicity avian influenza virus found in a duck in Taiwan.Segment-by-segment comparisons identified similarities with viruses from a duck in Wakayama, Japan; a white-fronted goose in South Korea; a duck in China; and a duck in Taiwan. Another comparison involved an environmental sample from Kagoshima, Japan.These findings relate to individual gene segments. They do not show that the complete virus passed sequentially through Bangladesh, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and China, nor do they establish how the infection reached Andhra Pradesh.Possible routes of introduction:Migratory wild birds can introduce avian influenza viruses into domestic poultry. Other possible routes include the movement of infected poultry, contaminated vehicles and equipment, contact between backyard and commercial birds, environmental contamination and gaps in biosecurity.The latest Anantapur outbreak warrants further investigation because the farm procured birds from Telangana, even though no fresh outbreaks had been reported there. Investigators will need to determine whether the birds were infected before arrival, whether the virus was introduced through subsequent contact, or whether it entered the farm through another route.Animal husbandry department joint director Dr Prem Chand said farmers had reported unusual bird deaths at poultry units operating under the National Livestock Mission in Anantapur. “Samples were sent to Vijayawada, where they initially tested positive for bird flu. The infection was subsequently confirmed by the laboratory in Bhopal. Poultry operations will remain suspended within a 1-km radius of the infected premises for three months. The area within a 10-km radius has been designated as a surveillance zone,” said Dr Prem Chand. supplementary_news.content: The sweeter side of veterinary medicine Welcome to your new favorite place to grow in vet med. Discover brilliant experts, engaging videos, interactive quizzes, inspiring stories, and podcasts that keep you curious, connected, and excited about what's next. After serving in the U.S. Navy, raising a family while earning her veterinary degree, and drawing inspiration from her immigrant mother's entrepreneurial journey, Dr. Lieu Balu is preparing to lead her own veterinary clinic in Phoenix. Scientists detect H5 bird flu antibodies in apparently healthy Greenland polar bears, raising new concerns about wildlife disease spread in the Arctic. Ask most people what a veterinary pathologist does all day and they’ll probably picture microscopes, slides, cells, and very serious diagnostic reports. Dr. Aleksandra Zuraw certainly does all of that. New research involving nearly 900 dogs reveals that larger breeds don't just have shorter lives. Their bodies may actually age faster at the molecular level, and the discovery could change how scientists approach canine longevity. H5N1 bird flu strikes Minnesota turkey and Indiana duck farms as another Texas dairy herd tests positive, raising new concerns for veterinarians. LMU researchers challenge a decades-old model: genetically modified embryos lacking interferon tau can establish pregnancies and develop into healthy calves. A landmark Purina study found that lean Labrador Retrievers lived 1.8 years longer and developed chronic disease later. Here's why the findings still matter for veterinarians 25 years later. Scientists warn that emerging African swine fever variants could undermine vaccine protection, making surveillance and biosecurity more important than ever. Letter of Reasonable Assurance clears the way for Maryland’s first in-state veterinary school to begin recruiting and admitting its inaugural class in 2027 11 careers. 6 questions. Zero chill. Veterinary medicine isn't one job—it's about eleven careers hiding under the same white coat. There is a conversation happening in break rooms, group chats, and parking lots all over veterinary medicine. It usually starts the same way. I love the medicine, but I do not know how much longer I can do this. And it usually ends with a quiet assumption that something is wrong with the person saying it. Somewhere along the way, veterinary medicine developed an unwritten rule: clinical practice is the real job, and everything else is quitting. It gets absorbed in school, reinforced in practice, and carried around as guilt by veterinarians who are exhausted, curious, or simply ready for a change but afraid that stepping out of the exam room means abandoning their oath. If you are graduating this year, the offers are probably already arriving, and some of the numbers are eye-watering. Signing bonuses have become the headline of new grad recruitment, and with student debt where it is, nobody could blame you for reading the biggest number and reaching for a pen. Vet school can turn almost anything into a performance metric. Grades, class rank, clinical skills, productivity, sleep, exercise, and sometimes even food can quietly become one more thing you feel like you should be “doing right.” Add long days, irregular schedules, stress, limited money, constant comparison, and a culture that can reward pushing through discomfort, and it is easy for a complicated relationship with food or your body to hide in plain sight. There are queer and trans veterinarians who came before you, students at other schools experiencing many of the same things, peer-support volunteers willing to listen, community organizations that know your city, and national groups that can help when a problem becomes medical, legal, academic, or overwhelming. Vet school has a way of eating your entire calendar. Between exams, labs, rotations, boards, jobs, relationships, and trying to get enough sleep to remain functional, personal health can slide down the priority list pretty quickly. There is a particular kind of kitchen alchemy that happens when nothing gets thrown away: a roast chicken becomes dinner, then lunch, then the broth for Thursday's ramen. A single Sunday afternoon becomes a month of breakfasts. What follows is not a diet plan so much as a system, one built on a $500 monthly grocery budget, a single person's appetite, and the stubborn belief that homemade is both cheaper and better. Meet Mecca Gladney, a first-generation college graduate, mother, and University of Arizona veterinary student pursuing a career in veterinary surgery while championing representation, mentorship, and mental health. The UC Davis veterinary student took a winding road to her dream school, but every setback helped shape the veterinarian and mentor she hopes to become. Now Monika Lagarejos wants to use her place in veterinary medicine to care for animals, strengthen communities, and make sure the next generation of future veterinarians knows they belong. McPaul Hermoso started veterinary school at 35 after earning multiple degrees and living in five countries. Discover his unconventional journey, lifelong dream of becoming a veterinarian, and mission to inspire others. From four years cheering at LSU to studying veterinary medicine at the Royal Veterinary College, Jalyne Blackwell is building a career by saying yes to the opportunities that scare her a little—and trusting that the unexpected path might be the right one. After France’s competitive exams shut the door, this 20-year-old found her calling 800 miles from home — and proof that a detour can still lead exactly where you were meant to go. Meet Taja Bell, an LSU veterinary student, Army Animal Care Specialist, mom and model working toward a future in emergency medicine and surgery. There is a particular kind of courage it takes to walk away from a career you have already proven yourself in and start over as a first-year student. Emese Avdeyenkova has done exactly that, twice over, once when she traded a biology degree for an Army uniform, and again when she traded that uniform for a white coat. Now she is bringing all of it, the discipline, the humility, and the hard-won perspective, to Vet Candy Radio as one of the vet student hosts of Vet School After Dark. America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer and her cat daddy husband Clay Palmer dig into the real science, history, and psychology behind humanity's longest-running obsession. We're talking ancient Egypt, where cats were literally worshipped as gods. We're talking the internet, where cats generate more content than almost anything else on the planet. From ancient worship to TikTok stardom, cats have clawed their way into our hearts and honestly, they never asked for permission. But why? What is it about the most indifferent creature on the planet that makes humans absolutely lose their minds? Think black cats bring bad luck? Think again. The truth about black cats is stranger, richer, and way more interesting than the superstition and Caitlin and Clay are here to set the record straight. In this episode of Cat Cafe, America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer and her cat daddy husband Clay Palmer dive deep into the wild world of cat mythology, feline folklore, and the weirdest cat superstitions that humans have carried for centuries. We are talking black cats across cultures — feared in some, worshipped in others. We are talking mythological cats from ancient Egypt to Norse legends to the shadowy corners of the internet. We are talking the real history behind the myths that still follow these animals into shelters today, where black cats consistently wait the longest for homes. Spoiler: the cats were never the problem. Think you know everything about cats? In this hilarious episode of Cat Cafe, America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer takes on the ultimate cat trivia challenge — and her cat daddy husband Clay is putting her knowledge to the test. From quirky cat facts to surprising feline science, this quiz will challenge even the most devoted cat lovers. Play along and see if you can beat America’s favorite veterinary receptionist, Caitlin Palmer! But it's not just fun and games. Every wrong answer comes with a punishment — and that punishment is pickle juice. Yes, really. Watch to find out who walks away victorious and who walks away regretting their cat knowledge gaps. • Fun (and tricky) cat trivia questions • Surprising cat facts you probably didn’t know • A very questionable pickle juice challenge Who’s the ultimate cat nerd... and who’s about to drink pickle juice? In this hilarious episode of Pet Candy, Caitlin and Clay go head-to-head in a cat trivia challenge with a twist—get a question wrong, and you have to take a sip of pickle juice Think you know cats? Play along and see if you can beat them (without the punishment.) Every NAVLE Warrior asks some version of the same question during week six: am I studying the right way, or am I just studying the most? Cognitive science has a real answer to that question, and it is not the one most students expect Every NAVLE study plan is built around content: which species, which systems, which diagnoses to drill. But the brain that has to hold all of that information is a physical organ, and it runs on three inputs: sleep, movement, and nutrition. Neglect any one of them and the same number of practice questions will produce worse results. Here's the science behind why, and what to actually do about it. Starting with the October to November 2026 testing window, the NAVLE looks different in two ways that actually matter for how you study. The exam moved to a new block format back in the spring update, and now the ICVA has also refreshed the Species and Diagnosis list itself, adding more than 100 diseases across the species you'll be tested on. That is not a small revision. That is the blueprint growing, and it means the way you have been prepping needs a second look. Paid NAVLE prep services can cost more than $600 for a thirty month pass, sometimes more. For companies selling them, that is a subscription. For a fourth-year veterinary student, that can be groceries for two months. And in a year when gas prices and food prices have squeezed every budget in America, plenty of vet students are doing math far scarier than anything on the exam. There are continuing education programs, and then there are continuing education programs where you accidentally debunk a mythical creature between bites of fried dough. World-First Breakthrough: Stem Cells from Cats Could Revolutionize Kidney Disease Treatment! Vet Candy has the details with Dr. Elan & Dr. Shannon. Big news in hemangiosarcoma research! Tune in as we cover a promising breakthrough that could change the way we approach this aggressive cancer. Inside: Dr. Wailani Sung helps you learn how to Recognize the Subtle Signs of Pain in Cats. Presented by Zoetis, maker of Solensia. SolensiaVetTeam.com A cat eye that won't heal is one of those cases that can quietly spiral into something serious — fast. In this episode of Rounds with Dr. Shannon, Dr. Shannon Gregoire sits down with veterinary ophthalmologist Dr. DJ Haeussler for a real clinical conversation about the feline eye cases that challenge general practitioners the most, starting with the corneal ulcer that just won't close. A limping dog walks into your exam room. The owner says it started two weeks ago. The leg looks fine. The X-rays look fine. Nothing adds up — yet. In this episode of Mystery Case Rounds, Dr. Shannon Gregoire walks through a real clinical case of canine lameness from the first exam to the final diagnosis, showing exactly how she thinks through a case when the answer isn't obvious. Photo: PR IMAGE PHOTO Cases of a new strain of bird flu were always expected to reach Australia's shores at some point, with the disease now detected across two states. A South Australian wildlife rescue centre where a migratory bird tested positive for H5N1 bird flu remained in lockdown as of Thursday. It comes after the nation's first two confirmed cases were reported near Esperance in Western Australia. Wildlife experts believe it is only a matter of time before further bird flu outbreaks. (HANDOUT/Esperance Wildlife Hospital and Sanctuary) Advertisement Ad WA Premier Roger Cook said there was always an expectation the strain would arrive in Australia at some point but the country had an advantage in detecting the initial cases relatively early. "In other countries, it's got into their poultry industry before they even knew it was their area - so the fact that we've got these early lines of sight is really important," he told reporters on Thursday. "We're doing a lot of work with the industry at the moment around what they need to prepare themselves for and how they need to respond." WATCH: Everything you need to know about the H5N1 bird flu strain Advertisement Ad Volunteers from the Wildlife Welfare Organisation SA collected the first bird to test positive in that state from Knights Beach, roughly 80km south of Adelaide, on June 14. Rescue centre manager Justin Biddle said the team decided to send samples for testing after being alerted to the positive cases in Esperance. "It otherwise looked pretty fit and healthy and it was actually doing quite well in care," he told AAP. "We can't stop migratory birds from entering Australia," rescue centre manager Justin Biddle says. (Dean Lewins/AAP PHOTOS) Advertisement Ad Mr Biddle said there had been no noticeable increase in unwell birds beyond what the organisation generally expected, but more cases appeared inevitable. "We can't stop migratory birds from entering Australia - which is who's going to be carrying it - and it's this time of year where the migratory Antarctic birds start hitting the southern coastline of Australia," he said. Scientists warn the threat of a slew of wild birds becoming infected is "more when than if". "It may not spread in this winter, but it could come from shorebirds ... in the next summer," BirdLife Australia president Hugh Possingham said on Thursday. "It'll probably get here eventually ... that's unavoidable. "The way migratory birds are coming to this continent from other continents and other places - something is going to happen." Three cases of H5N1 bird flu have been detected - two in WA and one in SA. (Susie Dodds/AAP PHOTOS) Advertisement Ad There was currently no threat to humans, federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins confirmed. "Chicken meat and eggs, as prepared normally, are perfectly safe to eat," she said. WA authorities have received almost 200 reports of sick birds since the first suspected case. Authorities confirmed on Wednesday another case of the strain had been detected in a southern giant petrel at Quindalup on the South West coast, north of Margaret River. The preliminary positive result has yet to be officially confirmed and a sample has been sent for further testing. Ground-based surveillance and drone surveys are being conducted at sea lion breeding sites along the South Australian coast, with testing frequency increased in high-risk areas. A temporary ban on all poultry products imported from Australia, imposed by Papua New Guinea's National Agriculture and Quarantine Inspection Authority on Monday, has been lifted. Conditions Bird Flu Hits Indiana Duck Facility and Minnesota Turkey Farm as Another Texas Dairy Herd Tests Positive Published Oct 13, 2026 3:44 AM EDT By Elena Vega YURI TUTOV | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket H5N1 avian influenza has struck two large poultry operations in the Midwest and another dairy herd in Texas, according to the latest federal data. The U.S. Department of Agriculture reported six new detections in the past week, CIDRAP reported, including a commercial turkey farm in Stearns County, Minnesota, with 34,400 birds and a commercial duck meat facility in Jay County, Indiana, with 24,300 birds. Federal officials also confirmed H5N1 in another Texas dairy cattle herd. All three cattle detections reported nationwide in the past 30 days have been in Texas. Texas confirmed its first infected dairy herd of 2026 in late May, after cows at a farm became sick and milk production dropped, and the farm was quarantined. Dairy detections matter because infected cows shed large amounts of virus in milk, which raises the exposure risk for workers in milking parlors and is a key reason federal officials stress pasteurization. The risk to the general public remains low, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The people most affected are those who work closely with infected animals, along with households that keep backyard birds or drink raw milk. New Detections in Three States Minnesota remains the center of fall activity. The state has reported eight affected commercial flocks and three backyard flocks in the past 30 days, with 343,050 birds affected, according to the USDA's flock detection tracker as summarized by CIDRAP. Stearns County is in central Minnesota and is home to St. Cloud. Nationwide, about 550,000 birds in 12 commercial flocks and nine backyard flocks have been affected over the past 30 days. Infected flocks are typically culled to stop the virus from spreading to other farms. The Indiana detection adds a second Midwest state to this fall's list of large commercial outbreaks. Jay County, in east-central Indiana near the Ohio line, has faced bird flu before this year. The Commercial Review reported two earlier detections in the county in March, including one at a commercial breeder duck facility. MedicalDaily previously reported that three more Minnesota flocks tested positive for H5N1 as fall waterfowl migration carried the virus south. Those outbreaks in Big Stone, Becker and Otter Tail counties affected about 118,000 birds. The newest detections move the virus into central Minnesota and Indiana and show dairy infections continuing in Texas. Low Public Risk, Higher Risk on Farms No new human infections with novel influenza viruses were reported to the CDC in the week ending Oct. 3, according to the agency's FluView report. The CDC continues to describe the current public health risk from H5N1 as low. The risk is different for people who handle infected animals. Poultry workers, dairy workers, farm families, veterinarians, and people who help depopulate flocks have the most direct exposure to the virus through birds, manure, milk, and contaminated surfaces. Most U.S. human cases since 2024 have occurred in people with that kind of contact. Farm workers who develop eye redness or irritation, fever, cough, sore throat, or muscle aches within 10 days of exposure should contact a clinician or health department and mention their work. Prompt testing matters because antiviral treatment works best when started early, and it helps public health officials track any change in how the virus behaves. Cooking poultry and eggs to safe temperatures kills the virus, and pasteurization protects milk. After an earlier Texas dairy detection this year, the Texas Animal Health Commission said FDA is confident that pasteurization inactivates H5N1 and that "the commercial, pasteurized milk supply is safe," according to FOX 7 Austin. Household Precautions During Fall Migration Most households do not need to change their routines. The practical steps apply mainly to people with animals or farm connections. Backyard flock owners should keep birds away from wild waterfowl, limit visitors, and report sudden deaths or illness to their state veterinarian or the USDA. Raw, unpasteurized milk carries a higher risk of exposure to H5N1 and other germs. Pet owners should keep cats away from raw milk, raw pet food made from poultry, and dead birds, since cats have been infected through these routes in past outbreaks. People who find dead wild birds should not touch them with bare hands and can report them to state wildlife officials. Hunters handling waterfowl this season should wear gloves, avoid eating or drinking while dressing birds, and wash their hands thoroughly afterward. Anyone with flu-like symptoms after close contact with sick or dead birds or livestock should tell a clinician about the exposure. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, or confusion needs emergency care. Federal Reporting and What Comes Next The USDA updates its livestock detection map each weekday. Fall and spring typically bring more poultry detections because migrating wild birds carry the virus along their flyways. Officials have not said how the Texas dairy herd became infected or whether nearby herds are being tested. The source of the Indiana duck facility infection has also not been publicly identified. MedicalDaily will continue tracking new poultry and dairy detections, any human cases reported by state health departments, and any change in federal risk assessments. Read more H5N1 Bird Flu Spreads to Poultry in 12 States, Raising Concerns Over Los Angeles Food Supply Ties to Central Valley Farms Bird Flu Detections Resume in US Dairy Herds and Poultry Flocks After a Month Without Federal Updates Seven Bird Flu Detections Since September 1 Hit Turkey Farms Across the Dakotas, Minnesota and Idaho Key Questions Answered Where was bird flu detected this week? The USDA reported H5N1 at a Stearns County, Minnesota, turkey farm with 34,400 birds, a Jay County, Indiana, duck facility with 24,300 birds, and a Texas dairy herd. How many birds have been affected recently? About 550,000 birds in 12 commercial and nine backyard flocks have been affected nationwide in the past 30 days, including 343,050 in Minnesota. Is H5N1 a risk to the general public? The CDC says the current public health risk is low. No new human infections with novel flu viruses were reported in the week ending Oct. 3. Who faces the highest risk? Poultry and dairy workers, farm families, veterinarians, and people with backyard flocks or close contact with sick animals face the greatest exposure. Is it safe to eat turkey, chicken and eggs? Yes, when properly cooked. Cooking poultry and eggs to safe temperatures kills the virus, and pasteurization makes commercial milk safe. What symptoms should exposed workers watch for? Eye redness, fever, cough, sore throat, or muscle aches within 10 days of contact with infected animals should prompt a call to a clinician or health department. How can backyard flock owners protect their birds? Keep birds away from wild waterfowl, limit visitors, practice good hygiene and report sudden illness or deaths to state animal health officials. supplementary_news.content: Sports Business News Life Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals ENVIRONMENT Jackie the Big Bear bald eagle died of bird flu, report finds Rene Ray De La Cruz USA TODAY NETWORK Oct. 15, 2026, 9:59 a.m. PT A post-mortem report revealed that the bald eagle Jackie died from a complex disease process. The primary cause of death was Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza, which led to a severe stomach ulcer. The ulcer caused internal bleeding, anemia, and a secondary bacterial infection. While an anticoagulant rodenticide was found in her system, it was not identified as the primary cause of death. The mystery surrounding the death of Jackie, one half of Big Bear Valley's famous bald eagle pair, has finally been answered. A newly released necropsy report found that Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza, commonly known as bird flu, was the primary underlying cause of the beloved eagle's decline and death. But wildlife experts say Jackie's case was unusual, involving a severe stomach ulcer, chronic blood loss, bacterial infection and multiple interconnected health problems that developed over time. The findings, released Wednesday by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance and Ojai Raptor Center, provide the most detailed explanation yet of what happened to the eagle known to millions of viewers who followed her life through Big Bear's popular nest cameras. What caused Jackie the Big Bear bald eagle to die? Veterinary pathologists determined Jackie was suffering from Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza, or HPAI, a virus that has circulated among wild bird populations across the United States in recent years. According to Steve Kubiski, director of disease investigations with the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Jackie's case presented in an uncommon way. Rather than causing the typical symptoms associated with bird flu, the infection triggered a severe ulcer in her ventriculus, the muscular portion of a bird's stomach, or gizzard. The ulcer caused persistent internal bleeding that led to severe anemia and allowed bacteria to enter her bloodstream, resulting in bacterial sepsis. The report concluded those conditions, combined with widespread inflammation and blood clot formation, ultimately led to Jackie's death. Necropsy reveals chronic illness and internal bleeding The examination found evidence of a long-developing disease process involving significant damage to Jackie's stomach tissue. Wildlife veterinarians said the ulcerated tissue caused ongoing blood loss and persistent anemia. Testing also detected bird flu virus genetic material in multiple organs and tissues throughout her body, including the damaged stomach tissue. Researchers ruled out several other potential causes. Follow-up testing found Jackie was negative for West Nile virus, and heavy metals, including lead, were within acceptable limits and were not linked to her illness or death. The findings helped explain many of the symptoms wildlife specialists observed while Jackie was receiving treatment after she was found injured near the family's nest in Fawnskin in July. Was rat poison responsible for Jackie's death? Testing detected brodifacoum, a common anticoagulant rodenticide often used to kill rats and mice, in Jackie's liver. However, the necropsy found no signs of the uncontrolled bleeding typically associated with rodenticide poisoning. Because of that, investigators concluded brodifacoum was not the primary cause of illness or death, though the report noted the presence of the toxic substance and other environmental contaminants in her system. What the report means for California's bald eagles Wildlife officials say the findings could help biologists and veterinarians better understand how bird flu affects raptors and other protected species. "The necropsy results have helped connect many of the findings we were seeing throughout the eagle's hospitalization," Ojai Raptor Center Executive Director Chris Eksteen said in a statement. California Department of Fish and Wildlife Director Meghan Hertel said understanding Jackie's case may help inform future treatment and conservation efforts involving bald eagles and other wildlife exposed to avian influenza. The report also noted that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's National Eagle Repository cremated Jackie's remains to reduce the risk of spreading bird flu to people or other wildlife. How are Shadow and the Big Bear eaglets doing? The report found no evidence that Shadow, Jackie's longtime mate, or their eaglets, Sandy and Luna, were sick. Since Jackie's death in August, Shadow has remained in the Big Bear area and has frequently been seen with a younger female bald eagle known as KD1, or Kaydee. Meanwhile, Sandy and Luna fledged earlier this year and entered the wild, giving a bright spot to thousands of eagle enthusiasts who followed the family online. supplementary_news.content: 今日动态 生物通首页 今日动态 新技术专栏 人才市场 生物通首页 > 今日动态 > 正文 尼日利亚活禽市场H5N1与H9N2禽流感病毒的检出及其溢出与重配风险 时间:2026年10月12日 来源:BMC Veterinary Research 编辑推荐: 摘要 背景 禽流感病毒(AIVs)包括高致病性H5N1和低致病性H9N2,构成了重大的人畜共患威胁。自2006年和2017年分别在西非首次检测到这两种亚型以来,它们已多次传入尼日利亚。本研究旨在通过2022年3月至11月对尼日利亚Hadejia和Kano活禽市场(LBMs 广告 X 欢迎领域“高通量小分子筛选解决方案”>> 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 “畅读会员”登录查看原文链接 Research Open access 摘要背景禽流感病毒(AIVs)包括高致病性H5N1和低致病性H9N2,构成了重大的人畜共患威胁。自2006年和2017年分别在西非首次检测到这两种亚型以来,它们已多次传入尼日利亚。本研究旨在通过2022年3月至11月对尼日利亚Hadejia和Kano活禽市场(LBMs)的主动监测,调查这些病毒目前的遗传多样性及其溢出风险。结果我们采样了219只禽鸟,每只采集两份拭子(共438份拭子样本)。只要至少有一份拭子检测为阳性,即判定该只禽鸟为阳性。在禽鸟层面,在Kano Sabon Gari活禽市场的125只表面健康的珍珠鸡中检测到3只(2.4%)高致病性H5N1。值得注意的是,低致病性H9N2的检出率显著更高,Hadejia活禽市场的94只鸡中有10只(10.6%)阳性。总体而言,219只禽鸟中有13只(5.9%)H5N1或H9N2检测为阳性。系统发育和选择压力分析确认,H9N2病毒属于G1谱系,其血凝素(HA)基因中携带关键的哺乳动物适应性特征,包括S143T、S145T和S121T,这些位点与对类似人类的α2–6唾液酸受体亲和力增强相关。系统发育分析显示,该H5N1毒株归属于2.3.4.4b分支,与导致2021–2022年尼日利亚疫情以及2023年初尼日尔后续暴发的病毒株具有密切的遗传关系。结论在尼日利亚不同的活禽市场中检测到了H5N1和H9N2。尽管这些发现并未提供当前共同循环或基因重配的证据,但在更广泛的活禽市场体系中同时检测到这两种亚型,加之H9N2中存在的推定哺乳动物适应性标记,凸显了潜在的基因重配风险——一旦这些病毒日后在同一市场内共同循环并感染同一宿主,就可能发生重配。因此,需要持续进行基因组监测,以发现未来的病毒趋同和新兴重配毒株,并为大流行病应急准备和防控策略提供依据。 打赏 欢迎领取《CGT 研发全流程解决方案》 展开全文 开通VIP 享海量文章 全站开放获取+解锁超过 200万篇新闻全文+每日更新 2000+篇,学术前沿动态全时追踪! It is increasingly a practical framework for protecting profitability, reducing resource losses and securing the future of animal protein production. ADM’s approach aligns with its Next Generation Thinking strategy, which focuses on helping customers improve resource efficiency, production performance, and environmental outcomes. For animal nutrition professionals, sustainability can be viewed through 3 connected pillars: economic, environmental and social sustainability. Economic sustainability is the foundation of resilient production systems. A farm, integrator or feed business must remain profitable to continue investing in better practices, new technologies and long-term improvement. Feed cost efficiency, lower mortality, fewer downgraded products, improved feed conversion and longer productive lifespans all contribute directly to that objective. Environmental sustainability focuses on producing animal protein while using fewer natural resources and reducing pressure on land, water, air and biodiversity. In feed, this means improving nutrient efficiency, reducing nitrogen, phosphorus and mineral excretion, limiting avoidable waste and responsible sourcing raw materials. ADM supports these efforts through traceability and responsible sourcing programs aligned with its ambition to develop deforestation – and conversion – free supply chains, particularly in areas identified as having a greater risk of deforestation and ecosystem conversion. Social sustainability completes the picture by supporting safe, transparent and responsible food systems. It includes animal welfare, food safety, responsible use of resources, and the long-term viability of the people, farms and communities involved across the agricultural value chain. Starting with economics: The SINCRO treasure hunt ADM’s SINCRO service offering is based on a clear principle: progress must be measurable. The journey therefore begins with economic sustainability. By analysing technical and economic results, SINCRO helps identify where value is being lost and where growth opportunities can be captured. This is especially relevant in an industry where small performance gaps can translate into significant financial impact at farm or feed mill level. This approach can be compared to a treasure hunt. In many production systems, hidden losses are present in the data: a slightly higher feed conversion ratio, marginally increased mortality, downgraded eggs, reduced animal longevity, or inconsistent raw material quality. Individually, these gaps may appear limited. When converted into economic value, however, they can reveal substantial sources of lost profit. ADM illustrates this logic through digital tools such as TreasurePerform, which helps convert technical gaps versus a reference into economic losses. A difference in feed conversion ratio, mortality, laying persistency or egg discard rate can be expressed in monetary terms, making priorities easier to discuss and decisions easier to make. This first diagnostic step creates the basis for targeted actions, combining services, expertise and solutions to improve technical performance and strengthen economic sustainability. From grain to farm: A holistic route to environmental sustainability Raw material sourcing has a major influence on the carbon footprint of animal feed. Using verified deforestation-free raw materials can reduce deforestation-related supply chain risk and may lower certain environmental impacts associated with feed ingredient sourcing, depending on the sourcing scenario and assessment methodology. ADM supports customers with traceable sourcing solutions and responsible supply chain programs designed to reduce risks linked to deforestation and conversion. Its soy strategy included traceability, supplier engagement, risk assessment and monitoring aimed at reducing deforestation and land-conversion risks within high-risk sourcing regions. As customers increasingly seek to quantify the environmental impact of feed ingredients, access to credible life cycle assessment (LCA) data has become an important component of responsible sourcing. ADM offers products supported by Global Feed LCA Institute (GFLI)-branded life cycle assessment data, including soybean meal and palm kernel expeller, enabling customers to make more informed sourcing decisions and support transparent environmental reporting. For palm kernel expeller, this verified data demonstrates up to a 25% lower carbon footprint compared with conventional alternatives, illustrating how ingredient selection can contribute to measurable emissions reductions across both the feed supply chain and livestock production. Precision nutrition is another practical lever for improving sustainability. It helps nutritionists formulate closer to animals’ real requirements while limiting excess nutrients and avoidable waste. This starts with accurate characterization of raw materials, including their quality and variability. Through SINCRO, ADM helps customers access laboratory analyses and NIR calibrations to support their quality control programs. ADM’s MatrixNutri app supports this approach by converting analytical results for more than 400 ingredients into precise, species-specific nutritional values, including values for aquaculture and providing a robust foundation for accurate feed formulation. Together, these services are designed to help reduce resource losses associated with formulation variability while supporting profitability thereby supporting both environmental and economic goals. A practical example can be seen in a broiler trial conducted by ADM in which crude protein in the finisher diet was reduced from 19% to 16.2% in parallel to specific adjustments. Final live weight was maintained, while total protein intake decreased. In this trial, modelling indicated that the carbon footprint of the finisher feed was up to 17% lower than the reference formulation. At farm gate, modelling indicated lower environmental impacts per kg of meat produced for the indicators assessed in the study. This illustrates how ADM’s nutrition expertise can help customers move beyond least-cost formulation toward a broader optimization model that integrates economic, zootechnical, and environmental objectives. ADM’s broad portfolio of feed additives and specialty solutions complements its grain-to-farm approach by helping customers reduce production losses and improve resource efficiency and farm performance. Improving eggshell quality, for example, can reduce the number of downgraded or discarded eggs. Supporting laying hen longevity can reduce the non-productive investment represented by replacement pullets. Improving sow robustness and reproductive performance can reduce culling and save resources. Organic trace mineral solutions, such as the B-Traxim range, can support mineralbioavailability, thereby contributing to lower mineral excretion. In this context, ADM’s Next Generation Thinking strategy is not positioned as an opposition between profitability and sustainability. Rather, it shows that both objectives can reinforce each other when data, nutrition expertise and field performance are connected. By reducing technical gaps, improving nutrient use and animal robustness, limiting waste and supporting responsible raw materials sourcing, animal feed professionals can create more efficient production systems that are economically robust and designed to use resources more efficiently and reduce production losses. Conclusion: Building sustainable value through measurable improvement For the animal feed industry, the most effective sustainability strategies are those that can be measured, implemented and translated into value. ADM’s approach starts with economic performance because profitability gives producers the capacity to invest, adapt and improve. From there, SINCRO connects control of raw materials, precision nutrition and performance monitoring to help reduce variability and unlock hidden opportunities. ADM feed additives and specialty solutions provide another practical lever, helping improve nutrient efficiency, animal robustness, product quality and loss reduction across species and production systems. Actions that improve farm profitability, such as better feed efficiency, fewer losses, stronger animal robustness, longer productive lifespans and more accurate formulation, can also lower the use of natural resources. Responsible sourcing and traceability help address environmental risks associated with key raw materials, including land-use change and deforestation, before those materials enter the feed mill. This holistic model shows that sustainability is not a separate agenda for animal nutrition, but an integrated process supported by ADM at each step of the value chain. By combining sourcing expertise, analytical tools, nutrition services, performance monitoring and tailored solutions, ADM can help customers build more competitive, transparent and resilient production systems for the future.Learn more about ADM’s SINCRO solutions here. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife said in a news release Wednesday that a necropsy and additional testing found that the primary underlying cause of Jackie’s death in August was highly pathogenic avian influenza. In the weeks leading up to her death she was being treated at the Ojai Raptor Center for a variety of ailments including anemia. (AP) — Bird flu caused the death of a bald eagle named Jackie who had become an internet sensation and a symbol of the species' recovery in California, officials said. A necropsy and additional testing found that the primary underlying cause of Jackie's death in August was highly pathogenic avian influenza, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife said Wednesday in a news release. In the weeks before she died, Jackie was being treated at the Ojai Raptor Center for various ailments, including anemia. For more than a decade, nature lovers watched via an online video feed as Jackie and her partner, Shadow, tended to their nest each year atop trees near Big Bear Lake in the San Bernardino Mountains east of Los Angeles. There's no evidence Shadow is ill, according to the news release. The nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley installed the nest camera in 2015 and documented the successes and failures of each breeding season. Highly pathogenic avian influenza has been circulating in bird populations throughout the U.S. While waterfowl and shorebirds are natural hosts for bird flu viruses, eagles and other raptors can be exposed through contact with infected birds or by eating them, according to the news release. Jackie's remains were cremated to prevent transmission of the virus, it said. American bald eagles teetered on the brink of extinction until the pesticide DDT was banned in the 1970s and other protections were established, leading the species to rebound and be removed from the federal endangered list. PDT by NWS San Diego CA 30 of 30 News Avian Influenza identified as primary underlying cause of Big Bear bald eagle Jackie’s decline Credit: The Ojai Raptor Center Jackie the bald eagle at the Ojai Raptor Center (7/29/26) By Jesus Reyes October 14, 2026 6:43 PM Published October 14, 2026 6:11 PM BIG BEAR, Calif. (KESQ) - The final necropsy report on Jackie the Big Bear bald eagle's death was released on Wednesday, revealing Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza as the underlying primary cause of her decline. "The necropsy, performed by veterinary pathologists at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, along with extensive additional laboratory and toxicology testing, provided new information about the complex medical condition that led to Jackie’s decline and death," reads a news release by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW). Jackie died on August 10 after more than three weeks of intensive medical care at the Ojai Raptor Center. Officials said the "necropsy revealed a complex and unusual disease process involving severe, chronic inflammation and ulceration of the stomach, persistent internal bleeding, anemia and secondary bacterial sepsis." Further diagnostic testing confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) within the affected tissues. HPAI is an infectious disease that primarily affects birds and has been circulating in wild bird populations throughout the United States, the CDFW reports. Waterfowl and shorebirds are natural hosts of avian influenza viruses, while eagles and other raptors may be exposed through contact with infected birds or by consuming infected prey. Officials identified HPAI as an underlying cause of Jackie's severe stomach ulceration. Multiple complications developed over time and ultimately contributed to her decline and death. "Jackie's necropsy confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline," said Steve Kubiski, Director of Disease Investigations, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. "In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis." The agency added that Jackie showed signs of chronic disease involving the ventriculus, the muscular portion of a bird’s stomach, commonly called the gizzard. The damaged and ulcerated tissue contributed to ongoing blood loss and her persistent severe anemia. It also allowed bacteria to enter the body, resulting in a serious secondary bacterial infection. Severe inflammation and blood clot formation were also found in the heart and several major blood vessels. Follow-up testing showed that HPAI virus genetic material was present in several tissues throughout her body, including the ulcerated tissue in the ventriculus. Together, the findings showed that Jackie was suffering from multiple severe and interconnected disease processes that had been developing over time and ultimately led to her decline and death. “The necropsy results have helped connect many of the findings we were seeing throughout the eagle’s hospitalization,” said Chris Eksteen, Executive Director of Ojai Raptor Center. “We are grateful to the many veterinary specialists, laboratories, wildlife agencies and partner organizations who worked alongside our team to understand her illness and provide her with the best possible care. Caring for her was an extraordinary privilege for our entire team.” Consistent with established procedures intended to prevent the transmission of HPAI to wildlife or humans, Jackie's remains were cremated by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s National Eagle Repository. A ministry team inspecting falcons kept in a veterinary center in Riyadh, which takes care of the birds that are usually used for hunting, discovered the cases, Saudi Press Agency quoted the ministry statement as saying. The ministry said the 37 falcons, including the five positive cases “were killed and burned.” Laboratory tests are being conducted to establish if the cases also test positive for the N virus — “the other component of the (bird flu) virus,” it added. In November the Kingdom banned all bird imports from neighboring countries. That decision came a day after Kuwait announced a bird stricken with avian flu in the country carried the deadly H5N1 strain, in the first case of its kind in the Gulf. Another bird was found to have the milder H5N2 strain. Scientists fear that the more the virus spreads, the greater the chance that H5N1 will mutate into a form that is easily transmissible between humans, making it capable of sparking a global pandemic that could claim millions of lives. The toll from the H5N1 strain of bird flu has climbed to 80 people worldwide since 2003. What are the reporting requirements for a work competition case? For a workers’ compensation case to be valid, you generally need: (1) to be a covered employee, (2) an injury/illness tied to your work, (3) timely notice to your employer and filing, and (4) medical proof that work caused or aggravated the condition. Missouri has some key rules if the injury occurs here: Most employers with 5 or more employees must carry workers’ compensation; construction employers usually must carry it with even 1 employee You must report the injury to your employer in writing within 30 days of the accident or of discovering a workârelated illness. You must file a formal “Claim for Compensation” with the Missouri Division of Workers’ Compensation, generally within 2 years of the date of injury, death, or last benefit payment. File using the Division’s Claim for Compensation form, which you can mail to the Division. Most states use very similar basic elements: Missouri? There is an employer–employee relationship (not an independent contractor in most cases). The employer is required to carry, or actually carries, workers’ compensation insurance. There is a real injury or occupational disease, documented by medical records. The injury arose “in the course and scope” of employment (happened while doing your job or due to job conditions, not a purely personal activity). A causal link exists between the work and the injury or the worsening of a preâexisting condition (direct cause, aggravation, acceleration, or precipitation). When should I report an accident and is this important to my case? What is the time limit? You should report a work accident to your employer as soon as possible. In Missouri, you generally must do this in writing within 30 days; this is very important for protecting your right to benefits. supplementary_news.content: Home latest pakistan world sports showbiz entertainment Royal business health Sci-Tech Food Fact Check Sci-Tech Videos shows Watch LIVE TV X Home Latest Pakistan World Sports Showbiz Fact Check Sci-Tech Videos Shows LIVE TV Viral Jackie the bald eagle died from avian influenza, California wildlife officials confirm Jackie, the bald eagle, died after a three-week health scare on August 10, 2026 By Web Desk | Published October 15, 2026 Jackie the bald eagle died from avian influenza, California wildlife officials confirm Jackie, the beloved bald eagle, whose cause of death has been revealed two months after her death in August. Jackie, who captivated millions online via a livestream of the aerie overlooking Big Bear Lake, shared with mate Shadow. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife has announced Jackie’s cause of death. The wildlife department on Wednesday, October 14, revealed that Jackie died from highly pathogenic avian influenza, also known as bird flu. Steve Kubiski, Director of Disease Investigations, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, who performed the necropsy, said, “Jackie’s necropsy confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline.” The infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anaemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis,” Kubiski determined. Testing revealed that rat poison was in her system, but officials ruled it out as the primary cause of her illness or death. She had been suffering from multiple diseases, according to the department. Jackie, the bald eagle, died after a three-week health scare on August 10, 2026. The bald eagle, Jackie, raised multiple eaglets in Big Bear Lake with her partner Shadow, living a life for 14 years. Jackie was hatched from an egg in 2012, near Bug Bear Lake, California. She is survived by Shadow and her last two chicks, Luna and Sandy, who was born in March. Jackie’s long-time mate, Shadow is reportedly in good health and remains in Big Bear, according to the statement issued by the Fish and Wildlife department. supplementary_news.content: ___ × Market Information Top Poultry Companies Expert Insights Blogs Regions Magazines Sign In Poultry Meat Egg Poultry Health Sustainability Poultry Future Chicken Marketing Summit Poultry Tech Summit Broilers & Turkeys Diseases & Health Avian Influenza Avian flu cases confirmed in poultry in 5 European states As the northern hemisphere fall reaches its peak, a handful of new outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza involving domestic birds have been reported, while further infections in the wild population have been detected more widely across Europe. Jackie Linden October 12, 2026 mashi_naz | Bigstock Article Summary Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) outbreaks involving H5 viruses have been confirmed in poultry across five European countries—Belgium, Bulgaria, France, Germany, and the United Kingdom—over the past month, with hundreds of thousands of birds affected and 316 total farm outbreaks reported across Europe in 2026. Five European nations have confirmed HPAI outbreaks in poultry involving H5 family viruses since September 2026 Bulgaria reported 41,000 affected birds across two farms, bringing the nation's 12-month total to 18 outbreaks 2026 European totals show 316 poultry outbreaks in 16 countries, compared to 729 outbreaks across 23 countries in all of 2025 H5N1 virus variant dominates confirmed cases, with Poland leading at 143 outbreaks, followed by Germany with 40 Wild bird infections continue spreading with 2,709 HPAI outbreaks logged across Europe in 2026, primarily involving H5N1 Over the past month, new outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in poultry involving viruses of the H5 family have occurred in Belgium, Bulgaria, France, Germany and the United Kingdom (U.K.). In Bulgaria, the H5N1 HPAI virus serotype has been detected at two more poultry farms in the central province of Plovdiv since mid-September, based on notifications to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH). Affected at the first premises were 8,000 mallard ducks, followed by around 33,000 laying hens at the second location in the first week of October. These bring the nation’s total over the past 12 months to 18. Also confirming to WOAH two recent infections with this virus variant was France. Both those affected were commercial flocks in the department of Maine-et-Loire, and started in the first week of September. The first involved 2,500 vaccinated ducks, and the second close to 10,000 breeding ducks that had not been vaccinated against HPAI. Three French outbreaks have been reported since the end of August, all in Maine-et-Loire, which is located in the western region of Pays de la Loire. Great Britain’s HPAI outbreak total in poultry has increased to 20 following the detection of the H5N5 virus in the first days of October. Testing positive was a small backyard flock on the Isle of Lewis, according to the same source. Part of the Western Isles, Lewis is located off the northwestern coast of Scotland. Meanwhile, the veterinary authorities of Belgium and Germany have each reported to WOAH outbreaks linked to the H5N1 virus in captive birds. The Belgian outbreaks affected around 450 birds in mixed flocks in the Limburg and Antwerp areas, while the German outbreak in the northeast of the country is reported retrospectively, having started in May. Farm outbreak total approaches 320 So far in 2026, 16 countries in the region have confirmed a total of 316 HPAI outbreaks in poultry, according to the latest update of the Animal Disease Information System from the European Commission (EC; as of October 7). The database monitors listed animal diseases in European Union member states and selected adjacent countries (but not Great Britain). At each of the affected premises this year, presence of the H5N1 virus variant has been confirmed. For comparison, 729 outbreaks in these flocks were reported by 23 countries during the whole of 2025. This year, Poland’s total remains the highest to date at 143 although it has not changed since May. Next come Germany (40) and France (23). Including backyard poultry, ornamental flocks, zoos, and similar premises, the EC’s System monitors HPAI cases in “captive birds” in a separate category. To date in 2026, 15 countries have notified the System of 123 outbreaks involving captive birds. During the whole of last year, 25 countries registered 175 outbreaks in this category with the EC. HPAI-related developments affecting Europe’s poultry sector Based on the changing HPAI situation in the region, Germany’s veterinary reference laboratory Friedrich-Loeffler Institute has raised the disease risk level for the nation’s poultry flocks. The risk is now seen as “moderate” for both the transmission of H5 viruses to poultry and captive birds directly or indirectly from the wild population, and between wild birds within the country. Last month, EU member states agreed with a proposal from the European Commission Directorate for Agriculture, DG Agriculture and Rural Development (DG-AGRI) to release funds from the agricultural reserve to compensate Italian farmers hit by previous HPAI outbreaks. EUR61 million (US$68 million) will be directed to poultry and egg farmers whose businesses were impacted by measures taken to control and prevent the spread of infection between September of 2022 and March of 2025. Payments must be made to the recipients by May of next year. More widespread HPAI cases in wild birds As of October 7, a total of 2,709 HPAI outbreaks in Europe’s wild population had been logged by the EC’s System by 33 countries in 2026. Of these, the H5N1 virus serotype was involved in around 2,660, while the rest were identified as belonging to the H5 group. Based on EC data, wild birds infected with the H5N1 variant have been recorded by Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden over the past month. Following a hiatus of around 18 months, the same virus was detected again on the Mediterranean island of Cyprus in September, according to a recent WOAH notification. The same agency has been notified about the first wild birds that have tested positive for H5N1 since the start of the HPAI “season.” Six birds were found dead at four locations in England. Over the past month, WOAH has been informed about seven wild birds in Iceland that have tested positive for the H5N5 virus serotype. Please reference surfaced articles to validate AI summary Explore DeeperDive Full Summary Jackie, a 14-year‐old bald eagle from Big Bear Lake, California, died in August 2026 after an atypical case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1), leading scientists to label her infection a “scientific mystery.” The mysterious death of Jackie, a beloved California bald eagle, has been blamed on complications from avian influenza, news that has left some experts puzzled. "Nobody knew this was even a probability," said Dr. William Bowerman. "Her case gave us more science than we were expecting." Among the oddities: The disease wasn't believed to be widely circulating, said Bowerman, a professor of wildlife ecology and environmental toxicology at the University of Maryland who has been studying bald eagles since the 1980s. Officials announced Oct. 14 that a necropsy performed on Jackie, who died in August after a weekslong illness that mystified her doctors, revealed "Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline," said Steve Kubiski, director of disease investigations for the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. Jackie lived in Big Bear Lake in Southern California and was about 14 years old when she died. For the past decade, a camera livestreaming her nest captured major moments in her life, including laying eggs, raising eaglets and coupling up with mate Shadow. The result of the necropsy was a surprise to experts closely following Jackie's case, said Bowerman. The highly virulent strain of bird flu H5N1, which spread around the world in birds among migratory pathways, was first documented to be wiping out American bald eagles in 2022, causing numerous deaths and nest failures. The virus is still circulating and can infect wild birds, including raptors like the bald eagle, but there isn't a widespread outbreak as of late 2026, Bowerman said. That's good news for bald eagles, but the toll from the outbreak on the overall population level of the once endangered species is still untold, he said. Just how Jackie contracted HPAI is "another scientific mystery," Bowerman said. How did Jackie get bird flu? The reason it was so surprising that Jackie had bird flu is because her illness didn't present with typical symptoms, Bowerman said. Symptoms in an eagle might include walking in circles, holding and moving its head unnaturally, and being unable to fly, the National Park Service said. "In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis," Kubiski said in an Oct. 14 summary of Jackie's necropsy. Also, there has been no active outbreak of bird flu in the area, according to Bowerman. Usually, obvious symptoms or multiple deaths of birds would be observed to signify H5N1 is sickening birds. "When you take a look up in Southern California, there was no outbreak of bird flu this year that they were seeing. California in the spring declared that it was no longer an impact to the poultry industry. So you would not expect that bird flu would have been the cause for her decline just based on her symptoms," Bowerman said. The necropsy would not have determined how she got it. Because it was an unusual presentation, it's not even clear when she may have been exposed. Bowerman said she could have gotten the virus in 2026, and a change in the disease progression caused it to appear differently, or she could have gotten it years earlier and it could have been lying dormant in her system until it flared up. How does bird flu spread in bald eagles? There are three main ways bald eagles and other raptors are thought to contract bird flu, according to Bowerman. They are: Drinking water containing bird poop with the virus. Spread between bald eagles in close proximity through inhalation. Preying on waterfowl such as duck and geese that are infected, or consuming birds that have died of it. This is thought to be a primary cause for bald eagles. Jackie may have eaten an infected duck or goose at some point. What Jackie's illness, death taught scientists Jackie was first taken from Big Bear Valley for treatment at the Ojai Raptor Center in July after she was seen in an altercation with other eagles. She was in critical condition but staff didn't know why. She first appeared underweight, with severe anemia and inflammation affecting her kidneys. Her medical team turned to several potential causes: lead poisoning, zinc toxicity, rodenticide poisoning, cancer. At one point she underwent a blood transfusion. "You would not have suspected bird flu," Bowerman said. In some ways, Jackie's unique illness and death has provided her medical team and scientists who study bird flu and bald eagles much more data to consider than any other eagle that has died from it, he said. That's because in a typical presentation of H5N1-caused demise, a bird would quickly be tested for the virus and immediately cremated upon a positive result. Though there hasn't been documented spread human-to-human, there is a chance the virus could mutate to enable such spread, so cremating the remains of infected birds ensures the risk of transmission is low. But because H5N1 wasn't an immediate suspected cause, many other tests and treatments were performed on Jackie that would not have been done on other birds, Bowerman said. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, October 15, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Breast milk-derived antibody preparation shields mice from influenza infection by October 15, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Breast milk-derived antibody preparation shields mice from influenza infection Filter Content Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A purified antibody preparation derived from pooled human breast milk has demonstrated broad antiviral activity in laboratory assays and meaningful protection against influenza in mouse models, according to a new study published in Science Advances. The product, known as LCTG-001, is a polyclonal secretory immunoglobulin A, or secretory IgA, preparation purified from breast milk collected from 120 donors through milk banks in Indianapolis and Pittsburgh. Yona Tugg and colleagues report that the preparation neutralized several medically important respiratory viruses in vitro, including respiratory syncytial virus, human adenovirus type 5, and both H1N1 and H3N2 strains of influenza A virus, raising the prospect of a mucosally delivered passive immunization strategy built from a renewable human biological resource. Secretory IgA occupies a distinctive position in the immune system’s defensive architecture. Unlike the circulating IgG that dominates blood-borne immunity, secretory IgA is the principal antibody class at mucosal surfaces, where most respiratory viruses first make contact with host tissue. It is produced locally by plasma cells in mucosal-associated lymphoid tissues and is transported across epithelial barriers by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor, which attaches a secretory component that stabilizes the molecule in the harsh enzymatic environment of the airway lumen. This dimeric, secretory-component-bearing structure allows secretory IgA to trap viruses in mucus, cross-link them at the epithelial surface, and neutralize them before they gain access to target cells. Because breast milk is a naturally enriched source of secretory IgA tuned by the maternal immune system’s extensive history of mucosal exposures, pooled milk represents a uniquely diverse polyclonal antibody repertoire. The breadth of activity observed in the new study reflects that diversity. In neutralization assays, LCTG-001 inhibited RSV, human adenovirus type 5, and two antigenically distinct influenza A subtypes, H1N1 and H3N2. The preparation also bound proteins and virus-like particles derived from H5N1 avian influenza viruses belonging to clade 2.3.4.4b, the lineage responsible for ongoing outbreaks in dairy cattle and sporadic human infections. Binding, however, did not translate into potent neutralization: against the H5N1 strain tested, LCTG-001 showed little neutralizing activity, and the authors did not test whether the preparation could protect animals against H5N1 challenge. The result illustrates a common distinction in antibody virology, where attachment to viral antigens does not necessarily correspond to functional inhibition of infectivity. Get Cold Relief Discover more Study Biology Get Cold Relief Track Pregnancy Pamper Your Baby Get Fresh Dairy The central in vivo experiments used mouse models of H1N1 influenza infection. Animals received two intranasal doses of LCTG-001, one administered two hours before infection and a second given 24 hours after exposure, a schedule designed to establish antibody at the mucosal surface both before viral entry and during the early phase of replication. Treated mice in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient backgrounds experienced reduced illness and less lung damage than untreated controls. The protective effect in antibody-deficient mice is particularly notable, because it demonstrates that the exogenously delivered IgA can function without support from the recipient’s own humoral immune system, a property directly relevant to patients with primary or secondary antibody deficiencies who cannot mount robust antibody responses to vaccination. Get Cold Relief An intriguing pattern emerged from the virological measurements in immunocompetent mice. Lung viral loads were lower in treated animals early in infection, consistent with direct neutralization of inoculum virus at the respiratory mucosa, but by later time points the viral loads in treated and control mice were comparable. Despite this convergence in viral burden, treated animals retained less lung damage and better lung barrier integrity throughout. The authors suggest several non-mutually-exclusive explanations for this dissociation between viral load and pathology. Early neutralization may reduce the initial burst of replication and the inflammatory cascade it triggers, setting the disease trajectory on a milder course even if residual virus eventually replicates to similar levels. Alternatively, IgA-mediated immune complex formation may redirect antiviral responses toward less tissue-destructive pathways, or the antibody may directly modulate inflammatory signaling at the mucosal surface. Discover more Milk Filter Content Shop Grooming Two additional laboratory observations may bear on the mechanism of protection, although their in vivo contribution remains unresolved. First, LCTG-001 inhibited influenza neuraminidase activity in vitro. Neuraminidase, the surface glycoprotein targeted by the antiviral drugs oseltamivir and zanamivir, cleaves sialic acid residues and facilitates the release of newly formed virions from infected cells; antibody-mediated inhibition of this enzyme could plausibly slow viral spread within the lung. Second, when complexed with influenza antigens, LCTG-001 stimulated human neutrophils in vitro, hinting at a capacity to engage innate effector cells through Fc-dependent mechanisms. Polyclonal IgA immune complexes are known to interact with Fc-alpha receptors on neutrophils and other myeloid cells, and such interactions can promote phagocytosis or antiviral effector functions. Whether either of these activities contributes measurably to the protection observed in mice is a question the authors flag for future work. Get Cold Relief The therapeutic concept underlying LCTG-001 is mucosal passive immunization, the direct delivery of ready-made antibodies to the respiratory tract rather than relying on the recipient to generate them through infection or vaccination. Passive immunization with monoclonal antibodies has become an established paradigm for several infectious and immunological indications, but most approved products are administered systemically and target a single antigen. A polyclonal secretory IgA preparation delivered intranasally offers a different profile: it acts at the portal of viral entry, it carries specificity against many epitopes simultaneously, and its polyclonal composition may reduce the risk that viral escape mutations abolish protection, since a virus would need to alter multiple antigenic sites at once to evade the full antibody mixture. The donor pool is central to that breadth. The 120 donors whose milk fed the preparation carry antibodies shaped by decades of infections and vaccinations across genetically diverse immune systems, effectively compressing a population-level antibody repertoire into a single therapeutic lot. Milk banking infrastructure, already established for neonatal nutrition, provides a practical collection channel, although scaling production to a level suitable for widespread seasonal or pandemic use would pose substantial manufacturing, standardization, and regulatory challenges that the current study does not address. The researchers position LCTG-001 as a candidate for two distinct applications. The first is prophylaxis and early treatment for individuals with antibody deficiencies, a population in which influenza and other respiratory viruses can cause severe, prolonged disease and in which vaccine responses are often blunted. For these patients, an intranasal product that works independently of the recipient’s B-cell function could fill an important gap. The second, more speculative application is broader public health use, either as a complement to seasonal vaccination or as a rapidly deployable countermeasure during the early phase of an influenza pandemic, when a matched vaccine is not yet available and a polyclonal preparation with activity against multiple subtypes could bridge the interval. The binding observed against H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b antigens, even without strong neutralization, suggests the donor repertoire contains antibodies to avian influenza determinants, though the functional significance of that binding remains to be established. Important caveats frame the findings. All in vivo results come from mice, and the dosing schedule used in the animal studies was tightly controlled, with antibody delivered both before and shortly after infection; real-world performance under less predictable exposure conditions is unknown. No human efficacy data exist, and the authors are explicit that efficacy in humans has not been established. The mechanisms linking early viral load reduction and preserved lung integrity to the observed clinical benefit, as well as the roles of neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil stimulation, remain open questions. Nevertheless, the study provides a proof of concept that a polyclonal secretory IgA product purified from pooled human breast milk can deliver broad antiviral activity at the mucosal surface and protect against influenza-induced illness and lung injury in animal models, establishing a foundation for the further preclinical and, eventually, clinical evaluation of breast milk-derived antibodies as mucosal therapeutics for respiratory viral disease.
